The **Odawa**[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ottawa_people#cite_note-1) (also **Ottawa** or **Odaawaa**[/oʊ ˈ d ɑː w ə/](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English")) are an [Indigenous North American](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indigenous_peoples_of_the_Americas "Indigenous peoples of the Americas") people who primarily inhabit land in the [Eastern Woodlands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indigenous_peoples_of_the_Eastern_Woodlands "Indigenous peoples of the Eastern Woodlands") region, now in jurisdictions of the northeastern [United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States "United States") and southeastern [Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canada "Canada"). Their territory long preceded the creation of the current border between the two countries in the 18th and 19th centuries.

Their peoples are federally recognized as [Native American](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Native_Americans_in_the_United_States "Native Americans in the United States") tribes in the United States and have numerous recognized [First Nations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Nations_in_Canada "First Nations in Canada")[bands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Band_government "Band government") in Canada. They are one of the [Anishinaabeg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anishinaabe "Anishinaabe"), related to but distinct from the [Ojibwe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ojibwe "Ojibwe") and [Potawatomi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potawatomi "Potawatomi") peoples.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ottawa_people#cite_note-2)

After migrating from the East Coast in ancient times, they settled on [Manitoulin Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manitoulin_Island "Manitoulin Island"), near the northern shores of [Lake Huron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Huron "Lake Huron"), and the [Bruce Peninsula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bruce_Peninsula "Bruce Peninsula") in the present-day province of [Ontario](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ontario "Ontario"), Canada. They considered this their original homeland. After the 17th century, they also settled along the [Ottawa River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ottawa_River "Ottawa River"), and in what became the present-day states of [Michigan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michigan "Michigan") and Wisconsin. They also occupied other areas of the Midwest south of the [Great Lakes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Lakes "Great Lakes") in what became the United States.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ottawa_people#cite_note-3) In the 21st century, there are a total of approximately 15,000 Odawa living in Ontario, Canada, and in Michigan and [Oklahoma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oklahoma "Oklahoma") (former [Indian Territory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Territory "Indian Territory"), United States).

The [Ottawa dialect](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ottawa_dialect "Ottawa dialect") is part of the [Algonquian language family](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algonquian_languages "Algonquian languages"). This large family is made up of numerous smaller tribal groups or "bands", which are commonly called a "Tribe" in the United States and "First Nation" in Canada. Their language is considered a divergent dialect of [Ojibwe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ojibwe_language "Ojibwe language"), characterized by frequent [syncope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Syncope_(phonetics) "Syncope (phonetics)").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ottawa_people#cite_note-oxford-4)

## Tribe name

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Odawa&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Tribe name")]

_Odawaa_ (syncoped as _Daawaa_) is believed to be derived from the [Anishinaabe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anishinaabe "Anishinaabe") word _adaawe_, meaning "to trade", or "to buy and sell". This term is common to the [Cree](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cree "Cree"), [Algonquin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algonquin_people "Algonquin people"), [Nipissing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nipissing_First_Nation "Nipissing First Nation"), [Innu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Innu "Innu"), Odawa, and Ojibwe. The [Potawatomi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potawatomi_language "Potawatomi language") spelling of _Odawa_ and the English derivative "[Ottawa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ottawa "Ottawa")" are also common. The Anishinaabe word for "those men who trade, or buy and sell" is _Wadaawewinini(wag)_.

[Frederic Baraga](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederic_Baraga "Frederic Baraga"), a Catholic priest and missionary in Michigan, transliterated this and recorded it in his _[A Dictionary of the Otchipwe Language](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A\_Dictionary\_of\_the\_Otchipwe\_Language?action=edit&redlink=1 "A Dictionary of the Otchipwe Language (page does not exist)")_ as _"Watawawininiwok"_, noting that it meant "men of the bulrushes", associated with the many bulrushes in the [Ottawa River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ottawa_River "Ottawa River").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ottawa_people#cite_note-5) But, this recorded meaning is more appropriately associated with the _Matàwackariniwak_, a historical Algonquin band who lived along the Ottawa River.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

Their neighbors applied the "Trader" name to the Odawa because in early traditional times, and also during the early European contact period, they were noted as intertribal traders and barterers.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ottawa_people#cite_note-6) The Odawa were described as having dealt "chiefly in [cornmeal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cornmeal "Cornmeal"), [sunflower oil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sunflower_oil "Sunflower oil"), [furs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fur "Fur") and [skins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skin "Skin"), [rugs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carpet "Carpet") and [mats](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mat "Mat"), [tobacco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tobacco "Tobacco"), and medicinal [roots](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Root "Root") and [herbs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herb "Herb")".[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ottawa_people#cite_note-burton-7)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ottawa_people#cite_note-8)

The Odawa name in its English transcription is the source of the place names of the Ottawa River, which in turn is the namesake of the city of Ottawa, [Ontario](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ontario "Ontario"). The Odawa home territory at the time of early European contact, but not their trading zone, was well to the west of the city and river named after them.

[Ottawa, Ohio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ottawa,_Ohio "Ottawa, Ohio"), is the county seat of [Putnam County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Putnam_County,_Ohio "Putnam County, Ohio"), developed at the site of the last Ottawa reservation in Ohio. There is also an [Ottawa, Kansas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ottawa,_Kansas "Ottawa, Kansas").

## Language

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Odawa&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Language")]

Main article: [Ottawa dialect](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ottawa_dialect "Ottawa dialect")

The Odawa dialect is considered one of several divergent dialects of the [Ojibwe language](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ojibwe_language "Ojibwe language") group, noted for its frequent [syncope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Syncope_(phonetics) "Syncope (phonetics)"). In the Odawa language, the general language group is known as _Nishnabemwin_, while the Odawa language is called _Daawaamwin_. Of the estimated 5,000 ethnic Odawa and additional 10,000 people with some Odawa ancestry, in the early 21st century an estimated 500 people in Ontario and [Michigan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michigan "Michigan") speak this language. The [Ottawa Tribe of Oklahoma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ottawa_Tribe_of_Oklahoma "Ottawa Tribe of Oklahoma") has three fluent speakers.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ottawa_people#cite_note-9)

## Early history

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Odawa&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Early history")]

### Oral histories and early recorded histories

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Odawa&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Oral histories and early recorded histories")]

[![Image 19](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2c/An_Indian_of_ye_Outawas_Tribe_%26_his_Family_going_to_War_by_George_Townshend%2C_4th_Viscount_and_1st_Marquess_Townshend.jpg/250px-An_Indian_of_ye_Outawas_Tribe_%26_his_Family_going_to_War_by_George_Townshend%2C_4th_Viscount_and_1st_Marquess_Townshend.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:An_Indian_of_ye_Outawas_Tribe_&_his_Family_going_to_War_by_George_Townshend,_4th_Viscount_and_1st_Marquess_Townshend.jpg)

Mid-18th century sketch of an Odawa family by British soldier [George Townshend](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Townshend,_1st_Marquess_Townshend "George Townshend, 1st Marquess Townshend")

According to Anishinaabeg tradition, and from recordings in [Wiigwaasabak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wiigwaasabak "Wiigwaasabak") (birch bark scrolls), the Odawa people came from the eastern areas of [North America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_America "North America"), or [Turtle Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turtle_Island_(North_America) "Turtle Island (North America)"), and from a region called [Dawnland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dawnland "Dawnland") along the East Coast (where there are numerous Algonquian-language peoples).

Directed by the _miigis_ (luminescent) beings, the [Anishinaabe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anishinaabe "Anishinaabe") peoples moved inland along the [Saint Lawrence River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Lawrence_River "Saint Lawrence River"). At the "Third Stopping Place" near what is now the [Straits of Mackinac](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Straits_of_Mackinac "Straits of Mackinac"), Michigan, the southern group of Anishinaabeg divided into three groups, the Ojibwe, Odawa, and Potawatomi.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ottawa_people#cite_note-hodge-10)

There is [archaeological](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archaeological "Archaeological") evidence that the [Saugeen complex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saugeen_complex "Saugeen complex") people, a [Hopewell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hopewell_tradition "Hopewell tradition")-influenced group who were located on the [Bruce Peninsula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bruce_Peninsula "Bruce Peninsula") during the Middle Woodland period, may have evolved into the Odawa people. The Hopewell tradition was a widely extended trading network operating from about 200 BCE to 500 CE. Some of these peoples constructed earthwork [mounds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mound_builder_(people) "Mound builder (people)") for burials, a practice that ended about 250 CE.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ottawa_people#cite_note-ONArch-11) The Saugeen mounds have not been excavated.

The Odawa, together with the Ojibwe and Potawatomi, were part of a long-term tribal alliance called the [Council of Three Fires](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Council_of_Three_Fires "Council of Three Fires").[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ottawa_people#cite_note-12) Together they fought the nations of the [Haudenosaunee Confederacy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haudenosaunee_Confederacy "Haudenosaunee Confederacy") (who came from the East) and the [Dakota people](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dakota_people "Dakota people").

In 1615 French explorer [Samuel de Champlain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_de_Champlain "Samuel de Champlain") met 300 men of a nation which, he said, "we call _les cheueux releuez_" (modern French spelling: _cheveux relevés_ (hair lifted, raised, rolled up)), near the mouth of the [French River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_River_(Ontario) "French River (Ontario)"). Of these, he said:

> Their arms consisted only of a bow and arrows, a buckler of boiled leather and the club. They wore no breech clouts, their bodies were tattooed in many fashions and designs, their faces painted and their noses pierced.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ottawa_people#cite_note-burton-7)

In 1616, Champlain left the Wendat villages and visited the _cheueux releuez_, who lived westward from the lands of the [Wendat Confederacy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wendat_people "Wendat people").[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ottawa_people#cite_note-hodge-10)

The _[Jesuit Relations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jesuit\_Relations "Jesuit Relations")_ of 1667 reported that three tribes lived in the same town: the Odawa, the Kiskakon Odawa, and the Sinago Odawa. All three tribes spoke the same language.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ottawa_people#cite_note-13)

### Fur trade

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Odawa&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Fur trade")]

Due to the extensive trade network maintained by the Odawa, many of the North American interior nations became known to Europeans by the names the Odawa used for them (exonyms), rather than by the nations' own names (endonyms). For example, these exonyms include _Winnebago_ (from _Wiinibiigoo_) for the [Ho-Chunk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ho-Chunk "Ho-Chunk"), and [Sioux](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sioux "Sioux") (from _Naadawensiw_) for the Dakota. From the early days of the colony of [New France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_France "New France"), the Odawa became so important to the French and Canadians in [fur trade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fur_trade "Fur trade") that before 1670, colonists in [Quebec](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quebec "Quebec") (then called [Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canada_(New_France) "Canada (New France)")) usually referred to any Algonquian speaker from the Great Lakes region as an Odawa. In their own language, the Odawa (like the Ojibwe) identified as Anishinaabe (_Neshnabek_) meaning "people".

The mostly highly prized fur was beaver, popular in Europe. Other furs traded included deer, marten, raccoon, fox, otter, and muskrat. In exchange the Odawa received "hatchets, knives, kettles, traps, needles, fish hooks, cloth and blankets, jewelry and decorative items, and later firearms and alcohol".[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ottawa_people#cite_note-14) Up to the time of [Nicolas Perrot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicolas_Perrot "Nicolas Perrot"), the Odawa had a monopoly on all fur trade that came through [Green Bay, Wisconsin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Bay,_Wisconsin "Green Bay, Wisconsin"), or [Sault Ste. Marie, Michigan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sault_Ste._Marie,_Michigan "Sault Ste. Marie, Michigan"). They allegedly did "their best to exploit" the tribes in those areas "who did not use the canoe, by bartering with them bits of iron and steel and worn-out European articles for extravagant quantities of furs". For example, "the Crees gave the Ottawas 'all their beaver robes for old knives, blunted awls, wretched nets and kettles used until they were past service.'"[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ottawa_people#cite_note-15)

### Wars and refugees

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Odawa&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Wars and refugees")]

[![Image 20](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/4/4b/Chief_Pontiac_%281%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail_unscaled)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Chief_Pontiac_(1).jpg)

Odawa warrior with [gunstock war club](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunstock_war_club "Gunstock war club")

The Odawa had disputes and warfare with other tribes, particularly over the lucrative fur trade. For example, the tribe once waged war against the [Mascouten](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mascouten "Mascouten"). In the mid-17th century the Odawa allied with other Algonquian tribes around the Great Lakes against the powerful [Mohawk people](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohawk_people "Mohawk people") (of present-day New York) and their Haudenosaunee allies in the [Beaver Wars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beaver_Wars "Beaver Wars"). The European introduction of guns and other weapons to some of their trading partners had disrupted the traditional balance of power in the region and changed economic risks and rewards. All indigenous peoples on both sides were disrupted or decimated; some groups, such as the Iroquoian-speaking [Erie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erie_people "Erie people"), were exterminated as tribes. But by the mid-17th century, the tribes were more severely affected by new infectious diseases than warfare. Lacking acquired [immunity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Immunity_(medical) "Immunity (medical)") to these European diseases, they suffered epidemics with high fatalities.

In 1701, the French colonists built [Fort Detroit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Detroit "Fort Detroit") and established a trading post. Many Odawa moved there from their traditional homeland of Manitoulin Island near the Bruce Peninsula,[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ottawa_people#cite_note-hodge-10) and [Wyandot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wyandot_people "Wyandot people") also moved near the post. Some Odawa had already settled across northern Michigan in the Lower Peninsula, and more bands established villages around and south of Detroit. Their area extended into present-day Ohio.

With movements of the tribes in relation to warfare and colonial encroachment, the tribes settled in roughly the following pattern: "Sandwiched between the French, in the north and west, and the English, in the south and east, the [Miami](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miami_people "Miami people") settled in present-day Indiana and western Ohio; the Ottawa settled in Northwest Ohio along the Maumee, the Auglaize, and the Blanchard rivers; the [Wyandot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wyandot_people "Wyandot people") settled in Central Ohio; the [Shawnee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shawnee "Shawnee") in Southwest Ohio; and the [Delaware](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delaware "Delaware") (Lenape) in Southeast and Eastern Ohio."[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ottawa_people#cite_note-tanner-16)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ottawa_people#cite_note-17)

In the mid-18th century, the Odawa allied with their [French](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/France "France") trading partners against the [British](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Kingdom "United Kingdom") in the [Seven Years' War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seven_Years'_War "Seven Years' War"), known as the [French and Indian War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_and_Indian_War "French and Indian War") in the North American colonies. They made raids against Anglo-American colonists. The Odawa chief [Pontiac](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pontiac_(Ottawa_leader) "Pontiac (Ottawa leader)")[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ottawa_people#cite_note-auto-18) has historically been reported to have been born at the confluence of the Maumee and Auglaize rivers, where modern [Defiance, Ohio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Defiance,_Ohio "Defiance, Ohio"), later developed. In 1763, after the British had defeated France, Pontiac led a [rebellion against the British](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pontiac's_War "Pontiac's War"), but he was unable to prevent British colonial settlement of the region.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ottawa_people#cite_note-19)

A decade later, Chief [Egushawa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Egushawa "Egushawa") (also spelled Agushawa), who had a village at the mouth of the [Maumee River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maumee_River "Maumee River") on [Lake Erie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Erie "Lake Erie") (where Toledo later developed), led the Odawa as an ally of the British in the [American Revolutionary War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Revolutionary_War "American Revolutionary War"). He hoped to build on their support to exclude European-American colonists from his territory in northwest Ohio and southern Michigan.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ottawa_people#cite_note-autogenerated203-20) The defeat of the British by the United States had a far-ranging influence on British-allied Native American tribes, as many were forced to cede their land to the United States.

Following the Revolutionary War, in the 1790s, Egushawa, together with numerous members of other regional tribes, including the Wyandot and Council of Three Fires, Shawnee, Lenape, and Mingo, fought the United States in a series of battles and campaigns in what became known as the [Northwest Indian War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northwest_Indian_War "Northwest Indian War"). The Indians hoped to repulse the European-American pioneers coming to settle west of the Appalachian Mountains, but were finally defeated.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ottawa_people#cite_note-autogenerated203-20)

In 1792 President George Washington sent Major Alexander Truman, his servant William Lynch, and guide/interpreter William Smalley on a peace mission to the tribes. Truman and Lynch were killed; Truman was apparently killed prior to April 20, 1792, at Lower Tawa Town, an Ottawa village (Ottawa, Putnam County Ohio). In a campaign during 1794, [Anthony Wayne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Wayne "Anthony Wayne") built a string of forts in the upper Maumee River watershed, including [Fort Defiance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Defiance_(Ohio) "Fort Defiance (Ohio)"), across the river from the site of Pontiac's birth. While the British had encouraged the Native American efforts, they did not want to get drawn into open conflict again with the United States and withdrew from offering direct support to the tribes. Wayne's army defeated several hundred members of the Indian confederacy at the [Battle of Fallen Timbers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Fallen_Timbers "Battle of Fallen Timbers"), near the future site of [Maumee, Ohio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maumee,_Ohio "Maumee, Ohio") and about 11 miles upriver of present-day [Toledo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toledo,_Ohio "Toledo, Ohio").

#### Raid on Pickawillany

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Odawa&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Raid on Pickawillany")]

In the winter of 1751–1752, [Charles Langlade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Michel_de_Langlade "Charles Michel de Langlade") began assembling an allied war party of Odawa, Potawatomi, and Ojibwe warriors who traveled to [Pickawillany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pickawillany "Pickawillany"). They attacked the village in mid-morning on June 21, 1752, and killed thirteen Miami men and captured five English traders. Down to as few as twenty warriors the Miami tried to negotiate terms of surrender, and Langlade promised to allow the Miami men to return home if they handed over the English. The Miami sent only three of the five Englishmen. When the Englishmen reached Langlade's lines, one of his men stabbed one of them to death, scalped the Englishman, and ripped his heart out and ate it in front of the Miami men. Langlade's men seized the Miami chief [Memeskia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Memeskia "Memeskia"). He was killed, boiled and eaten in front of his warriors. Afterward the Odawa released the Miami women and left for Detroit with four captured Englishmen and more than $300,000 worth (in today's dollars[_[when?](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Manual\_of\_Style/Dates\_and\_numbers#Chronological\_items "Wikipedia:Manual of Style/Dates and numbers")_]) of trade goods.

This French-led victory over the English is believed to have led to the French and Indian War and contributed to the Seven Years' War on the European continent.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ottawa_people#cite_note-21)

### Treaties and removals

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Odawa&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Treaties and removals")]

In 1795, under the [Treaty of Greenville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Greenville "Treaty of Greenville"), the Odawa and other members of the Western Confederacy ceded all of Ohio to the United States, except the northwest area. This was part of the area controlled by the Detroit Odawa.

In 1807, the Detroit Odawa joined three other tribes, the Ojibwe, Potawatomi and [Wyandot people](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wyandot_people "Wyandot people"), in signing the [Treaty of Detroit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Detroit "Treaty of Detroit") under pressure from the United States. The agreement, between the tribes and [William Hull](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Hull "William Hull"), representing the [Michigan Territory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michigan_Territory "Michigan Territory"), gave the United States a large portion of today's [Southeastern Michigan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeastern_Michigan "Southeastern Michigan") and a section of northwest [Ohio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ohio "Ohio") near the Maumee River.

Many Odawa bands moved away from the European Americans into northern Michigan. The tribes retained communal control of relatively small pockets of land in the territory of the Maumee River.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ottawa_people#cite_note-WDL-22) Bands of Odawa-occupied areas are known as Roche de Boeuf[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ottawa_people#cite_note-23) and Wolf Rapids on the upper Maumee River.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ottawa_people#cite_note-sultzman-24)

In 1817, in the first treaty involving land cessions after the War of 1812, the Ohio Odawa ceded their lands, accepting [reservations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_historical_Indian_reservations_in_the_United_States "List of historical Indian reservations in the United States") at [Blanchard's Creek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blanchard's_Fork_Reserve,_Ohio "Blanchard's Fork Reserve, Ohio") and the [Little Auglaize River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Little_Auglaize_River "Little Auglaize River") in Ohio (a total of 34 square miles or 88 square kilometres). These were only reserves, for which they were paid annuities for ten years. Pressure continued to build against the Odawa as European-American settlers moved into the area.

After passage of the [Indian Removal Act of 1830](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Removal_Act_of_1830 "Indian Removal Act of 1830"), the US government arranged for the Odawa to cede their reserves in 1831. The four following bands eventually all removed to areas of Kansas, then part of [Indian Territory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Territory "Indian Territory"): the Blanchard's Creek, Little Auglaize, Roche de Boeuf, and Wolf Rapids bands.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ottawa_people#cite_note-sultzman-24)

## Modern history

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Odawa&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Modern history")]

The population of the different Odawa groups has been estimated. In 1906, the Ojibwe and Odawa on [Manitoulin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manitoulin_Island "Manitoulin Island") and [Cockburn Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cockburn_Island_(Ontario) "Cockburn Island (Ontario)") were 1,497, of whom about half were Odawa. There were 197 Odawa listed as associated with the Seneca School in Oklahoma, where some Odawa had settled after the American Civil War. In 1900 in Michigan there were 5,587 scattered Ojibwe and Odawa, of whom about two-thirds are Odawa.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ottawa_people#cite_note-hodge-10)

In the early 21st century, the total number of enrolled members of the federally recognized [Ottawa Tribe of Oklahoma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ottawa_Tribe_of_Oklahoma "Ottawa Tribe of Oklahoma") numbers about 4,700. There are about 10,000 persons who identify as Odawa in the United States, with the majority in Michigan. Another several thousand live in Ontario, Canada.

There has been one major anthropological study of the [Grand Traverse Band of Ottawa and Chippewa Indians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Traverse_Band_of_Ottawa_and_Chippewa_Indians "Grand Traverse Band of Ottawa and Chippewa Indians"). [Jane Willetts Ettawageshik](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jane_Willets_Ettawageshik "Jane Willets Ettawageshik") devoted approximately two years of study in the Grand Traverse Band of Ottawa and Chippewa Indians community. [Ettawageshik](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jane_Willets_Ettawageshik "Jane Willets Ettawageshik") recorded [Anishinaabe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anishinaabe "Anishinaabe") stories that speak of how the Anishinaabe people related to their land, to their people, and various other means of communicating their values, outlooks and histories in and around Northern Michigan. These stories have been translated into English by Howard Webkamigada and published as the book _Ottawa Stories from the Springs_.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ottawa_people#cite_note-25)

## Notable Odawa people

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Odawa&action=edit&section=18 "Edit section: Notable Odawa people")]

[![Image 21](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/3d/Pontiac_conspiracy.jpg/250px-Pontiac_conspiracy.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Pontiac_conspiracy.jpg)

Odawa Chief [Pontiac](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pontiac_(Ottawa_leader) "Pontiac (Ottawa leader)")[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ottawa_people#cite_note-auto-18) speaking at a council on April 27, 1763, 19th-century engraving.

*   [Jean-Baptiste Assiginack](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean-Baptiste_Assiginack "Jean-Baptiste Assiginack") (1768–1866), chief and public servant
*   [Andrew Blackbird](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Blackbird "Andrew Blackbird") (c. 1814/1817–1908), tribal leader, historian, and author of tribal histories
*   [Kelly Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kelly_Church "Kelly Church") (born 1967), black ash basket weaver and birch bark biter
*   [Cobmoosa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cobmoosa "Cobmoosa") (1768–1866), chief
*   [Egushawa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Egushawa "Egushawa") (c. 1726–1796), war chief
*   [Enmegahbowh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enmegahbowh "Enmegahbowh") (c. 1807–1902), first Native American to be ordained as an Episcopal priest
*   [Magdelaine Laframboise](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magdelaine_Laframboise "Magdelaine Laframboise") (1780–1846), Odawa-French fur trader and businesswoman, also supported public education for children on Mackinac Island; added in 1984 to Michigan's Women's Hall of Fame
*   [Daphne Odjig](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daphne_Odjig "Daphne Odjig") (1919–2016), [Woodlands style](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Woodlands_style "Woodlands style") painter and member of the [Indian Group of Seven](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Group_of_Seven "Indian Group of Seven")
*   [Petosegay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Petosegay "Petosegay") (1787–1885), merchant and fur trader
*   [Pontiac](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pontiac_(Ottawa_leader) "Pontiac (Ottawa leader)") (c. 1720–1769), chief. Leader of [Pontiac's War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pontiac's_War "Pontiac's War") against British and Americans
*   [Wawatam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wawatam "Wawatam") (fl. 1762–1764), chief

**Otawa** is a rural area in the [Western Bay of Plenty District](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_Bay_of_Plenty_District "Western Bay of Plenty District") and [Bay of Plenty Region](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bay_of_Plenty_Region "Bay of Plenty Region") of New Zealand's [North Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Island "North Island"). The Otawa Scenic Reserve has several walking tracks varying between 30 minutes and four hours return.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Otawa#cite_note-6) The tracks are described as advanced.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Otawa#cite_note-7) The peak of Otawa is 565 metres.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Otawa#cite_note-8)

## Demographics

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Otawa&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Demographics")]

Otawa statistical area covers 152.28 km 2 (58.80 sq mi) north, west and southwest of Te Puke.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Otawa#cite_note-Area-4) It had an estimated population of 2,390 as of June 2025,[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Otawa#cite_note-NZ_population_data_2023_SA2-5) with a population density of 16 people per km 2.

Otawa had a population of 2,130 in the [2023 New Zealand census](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_New_Zealand_census "2023 New Zealand census"), an increase of 147 people (7.4%) since the [2018 census](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2018_New_Zealand_census "2018 New Zealand census"), and an increase of 354 people (19.9%) since the [2013 census](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2013_New_Zealand_census "2013 New Zealand census"). There were 1,101 males, 1,023 females, and 9 people of [other genders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-binary_gender "Non-binary gender") in 693 dwellings.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Otawa#cite_note-11) 3.2% of people identified as [LGBTIQ+](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LGBTQ "LGBTQ"). The median age was 42.4 years (compared with 38.1 years nationally). There were 411 people (19.3%) aged under 15 years, 360 (16.9%) aged 15 to 29, 993 (46.6%) aged 30 to 64, and 366 (17.2%) aged 65 or older.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Otawa#cite_note-Census_2023-9)

People could identify as more than one ethnicity. The results were 86.3% [European](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_New_Zealanders "European New Zealanders") ([Pākehā](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P%C4%81keh%C4%81 "Pākehā")); 18.0% [Māori](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M%C4%81ori_people "Māori people"); 3.1% [Pasifika](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pasifika_New_Zealanders "Pasifika New Zealanders"); 6.2% [Asian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asian_New_Zealanders "Asian New Zealanders"); 0.7% Middle Eastern, Latin American and African New Zealanders (MELAA); and 2.3% other, which includes people giving their ethnicity as "New Zealander". English was spoken by 95.9%, Māori by 3.9%, Samoan by 0.6%, and other languages by 10.0%. No language could be spoken by 2.0% (e.g. too young to talk). [New Zealand Sign Language](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand_Sign_Language "New Zealand Sign Language") was known by 0.3%. The percentage of people born overseas was 16.1, compared with 28.8% nationally.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Otawa#cite_note-Census_2023-9)

Religious affiliations were 26.3% [Christian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christianity_in_New_Zealand "Christianity in New Zealand"), 0.4% [Hindu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hinduism_in_New_Zealand "Hinduism in New Zealand"), 1.8% [Māori religious beliefs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M%C4%81ori_religious_beliefs "Māori religious beliefs"), 0.8% [Buddhist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buddhism_in_New_Zealand "Buddhism in New Zealand"), 0.7% [New Age](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Age "New Age"), and 4.6% other religions. People who answered that they had [no religion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Irreligion_in_New_Zealand "Irreligion in New Zealand") were 55.6%, and 9.9% of people did not answer the census question.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Otawa#cite_note-Census_2023-9)

Of those at least 15 years old, 285 (16.6%) people had a bachelor's or higher degree, 1,038 (60.4%) had a post-high school certificate or diploma, and 396 (23.0%) people exclusively held high school qualifications. The median income was $45,900, compared with $41,500 nationally. 228 people (13.3%) earned over $100,000 compared to 12.1% nationally. The employment status of those at least 15 was 927 (53.9%) full-time, 285 (16.6%) part-time, and 51 (3.0%) unemployed.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Otawa#cite_note-Census_2023-9)

**Otawa** is a rural area in the [Western Bay of Plenty District](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_Bay_of_Plenty_District "Western Bay of Plenty District") and [Bay of Plenty Region](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bay_of_Plenty_Region "Bay of Plenty Region") of New Zealand's [North Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Island "North Island"). The Otawa Scenic Reserve has several walking tracks varying between 30 minutes and four hours return.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Otawa#cite_note-6) The tracks are described as advanced.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Otawa#cite_note-7) The peak of Otawa is 565 metres.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Otawa#cite_note-8)

## Demographics

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Otawa&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Demographics")]

Otawa statistical area covers 152.28 km 2 (58.80 sq mi) north, west and southwest of Te Puke.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Otawa#cite_note-Area-4) It had an estimated population of 2,390 as of June 2025,[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Otawa#cite_note-NZ_population_data_2023_SA2-5) with a population density of 16 people per km 2.

| The 2006 population is for a smaller area of 151.68 km 2. Source: [[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Otawa#cite_note-Census_2023-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Otawa#cite_note-Census_2018-10) |

Otawa had a population of 2,130 in the [2023 New Zealand census](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_New_Zealand_census "2023 New Zealand census"), an increase of 147 people (7.4%) since the [2018 census](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2018_New_Zealand_census "2018 New Zealand census"), and an increase of 354 people (19.9%) since the [2013 census](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2013_New_Zealand_census "2013 New Zealand census"). There were 1,101 males, 1,023 females, and 9 people of [other genders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-binary_gender "Non-binary gender") in 693 dwellings.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Otawa#cite_note-11) 3.2% of people identified as [LGBTIQ+](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LGBTQ "LGBTQ"). The median age was 42.4 years (compared with 38.1 years nationally). There were 411 people (19.3%) aged under 15 years, 360 (16.9%) aged 15 to 29, 993 (46.6%) aged 30 to 64, and 366 (17.2%) aged 65 or older.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Otawa#cite_note-Census_2023-9)

People could identify as more than one ethnicity. The results were 86.3% [European](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_New_Zealanders "European New Zealanders") ([Pākehā](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P%C4%81keh%C4%81 "Pākehā")); 18.0% [Māori](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M%C4%81ori_people "Māori people"); 3.1% [Pasifika](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pasifika_New_Zealanders "Pasifika New Zealanders"); 6.2% [Asian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asian_New_Zealanders "Asian New Zealanders"); 0.7% Middle Eastern, Latin American and African New Zealanders (MELAA); and 2.3% other, which includes people giving their ethnicity as "New Zealander". English was spoken by 95.9%, Māori by 3.9%, Samoan by 0.6%, and other languages by 10.0%. No language could be spoken by 2.0% (e.g. too young to talk). [New Zealand Sign Language](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand_Sign_Language "New Zealand Sign Language") was known by 0.3%. The percentage of people born overseas was 16.1, compared with 28.8% nationally.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Otawa#cite_note-Census_2023-9)

Religious affiliations were 26.3% [Christian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christianity_in_New_Zealand "Christianity in New Zealand"), 0.4% [Hindu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hinduism_in_New_Zealand "Hinduism in New Zealand"), 1.8% [Māori religious beliefs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M%C4%81ori_religious_beliefs "Māori religious beliefs"), 0.8% [Buddhist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buddhism_in_New_Zealand "Buddhism in New Zealand"), 0.7% [New Age](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Age "New Age"), and 4.6% other religions. People who answered that they had [no religion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Irreligion_in_New_Zealand "Irreligion in New Zealand") were 55.6%, and 9.9% of people did not answer the census question.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Otawa#cite_note-Census_2023-9)

Of those at least 15 years old, 285 (16.6%) people had a bachelor's or higher degree, 1,038 (60.4%) had a post-high school certificate or diploma, and 396 (23.0%) people exclusively held high school qualifications. The median income was $45,900, compared with $41,500 nationally. 228 people (13.3%) earned over $100,000 compared to 12.1% nationally. The employment status of those at least 15 was 927 (53.9%) full-time, 285 (16.6%) part-time, and 51 (3.0%) unemployed.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Otawa#cite_note-Census_2023-9)

**Saint Paul** (often abbreviated to **St. Paul**) is the [capital city](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_capitals_in_the_United_States "List of capitals in the United States") of the [U.S. state](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._state "U.S. state") of [Minnesota](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minnesota "Minnesota") and the [county seat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/County_seat "County seat") of [Ramsey County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramsey_County,_Minnesota "Ramsey County, Minnesota").[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Paul,_Minnesota#cite_note-StP_RC_MMSP-6) As of the [2020 census](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_census "2020 United States census"), the city had a population of 311,527, making it Minnesota's [second-most populous city](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_cities_in_Minnesota "List of cities in Minnesota") and the [69th-most populous](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_United_States_cities_by_population "List of United States cities by population") in the United States. Saint Paul and neighboring [Minneapolis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minneapolis "Minneapolis") form the core of the [Twin Cities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Twin_Cities "Twin Cities") metropolitan area, the third most populous in the [Midwest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Midwestern_United_States "Midwestern United States") with around 3.7 million residents.

The [Minnesota State Capitol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minnesota_State_Capitol "Minnesota State Capitol") and the state government offices sit on a hill next to downtown Saint Paul overlooking a bend in the [Mississippi River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mississippi_River "Mississippi River"). Local cultural offerings include the [Science Museum of Minnesota](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Science_Museum_of_Minnesota "Science Museum of Minnesota"), the [Ordway Center for the Performing Arts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ordway_Center_for_the_Performing_Arts "Ordway Center for the Performing Arts"), and the [Minnesota History Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minnesota_History_Center "Minnesota History Center"). Three of the region's professional sports teams play in Saint Paul: the [Minnesota Wild](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minnesota_Wild "Minnesota Wild") and [Frost](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minnesota_Frost "Minnesota Frost") (at the [Grand Casino Arena](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Casino_Arena "Grand Casino Arena")) and [Minnesota United FC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minnesota_United_FC "Minnesota United FC") (at [Allianz Field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allianz_Field "Allianz Field")). The minor-league baseball team the [St. Paul Saints](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Paul_Saints "St. Paul Saints") play at [CHS Field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CHS_Field "CHS Field"), 10 miles (16 km) from their major-league affiliate the [Minnesota Twins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minnesota_Twins "Minnesota Twins") in downtown Minneapolis.

The Legislative Assembly of the [Minnesota Territory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minnesota_Territory "Minnesota Territory") established the Town of Saint Paul as its capital near existing [Dakota Sioux](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dakota_people "Dakota people") settlements in November 1849. Named after a [log chapel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Cathedral_of_Saint_Paul_(Minnesota) "First Cathedral of Saint Paul (Minnesota)") established by [Lucien Galtier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucien_Galtier "Lucien Galtier"), it remained a town until 1854. The city rose to prominence as the headquarters of 19th-century industrialist [James J. Hill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_J._Hill "James J. Hill")'s railroad empire, with his transcontinental [Great Northern Railway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Northern_Railway_(U.S.) "Great Northern Railway (U.S.)") then one of the nation's most dominant. Saint Paul has a [mayor–council government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayor%E2%80%93council_government "Mayor–council government"). The mayor is [Kaohly Her](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kaohly_Her "Kaohly Her"), who took office in 2026.

[![Image 21](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/bb/Indian_Mounds_park.jpg/250px-Indian_Mounds_park.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Indian_Mounds_park.jpg)

A burial mound at [Indian Mounds Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Mounds_Park_(Saint_Paul,_Minnesota) "Indian Mounds Park (Saint Paul, Minnesota)")

Burial mounds in present-day [Indian Mounds Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Mounds_Park_(Saint_Paul,_Minnesota) "Indian Mounds Park (Saint Paul, Minnesota)") suggest the area was inhabited by the [Hopewell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hopewell_tradition "Hopewell tradition") Native Americans about 2,000 years ago.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Paul,_Minnesota#cite_note-Trimble-7)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Paul,_Minnesota#cite_note-8) From the early 17th century to 1837, the [Mdewakanton Dakota](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mdewakanton "Mdewakanton"), a band of the [Dakota people](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dakota_people "Dakota people"), lived near the mounds at the village of [Kaposia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kaposia "Kaposia") and consider the area encompassing present-day Saint Paul [Bdóte](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bd%C3%B3te "Bdóte"), the site of creation for their people.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Paul,_Minnesota#cite_note-Trimble-7)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Paul,_Minnesota#cite_note-DakotaLife-9) The Dakota called the area _Imniza-Ska_ ('white cliffs') for its exposed white sandstone cliffs on the river's eastern side.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Paul,_Minnesota#cite_note-10)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Paul,_Minnesota#cite_note-NPS-11) The Imniza-Ska were full of caves that were useful to the Dakota. The explorer [Jonathan Carver](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jonathan_Carver "Jonathan Carver") documented the historic Wakan Tipi in the bluff below the burial mounds in 1767. In the [Menominee language](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menominee_language "Menominee language") Saint Paul was called _Sāēnepān-Menīkān_, which means 'ribbon, silk or satin village', suggesting its role in trade throughout the region after the introduction of European goods.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Paul,_Minnesota#cite_note-12)

After the 1803 [Louisiana Purchase](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louisiana_Purchase "Louisiana Purchase"), U.S. Army Lieutenant [Zebulon Pike](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zebulon_Pike "Zebulon Pike") negotiated approximately 100,000 acres (40,000 ha; 160 sq mi) of land from the indigenous Dakota in 1805 to establish a fort. A military reservation was intended for the confluence of the [Mississippi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mississippi_River "Mississippi River") and [Minnesota rivers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minnesota_River "Minnesota River") on both sides of the Mississippi up to [Saint Anthony Falls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Anthony_Falls "Saint Anthony Falls"). All of what is now the Highland Park neighborhood was included in this. Pike planned a second military reservation at the confluence of the [St. Croix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Croix_River_(Wisconsin%E2%80%93Minnesota) "St. Croix River (Wisconsin–Minnesota)") and Mississippi rivers.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Paul,_Minnesota#cite_note-13) In 1819, [Fort Snelling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Snelling "Fort Snelling") was built at the Minnesota and Mississippi confluence. The 1837 Treaty with the Sioux ceded all tribal lands east of the Mississippi to the U.S. government.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Paul,_Minnesota#cite_note-14)[Chief Little Crow III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taoyateduta "Taoyateduta") moved his village, [Kaposia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kaposia "Kaposia"), from south of Mounds Park across the river a few miles onto Dakota land.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Paul,_Minnesota#cite_note-15)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Paul,_Minnesota#cite_note-16) Fur traders, explorers, and settlers came to the area for the fort's security. Many were [French-Canadians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French-Canadians "French-Canadians") who predated American pioneers by some time. A whiskey trade flourished among the squatters and the fort's commander evicted them all from the fort's reservation. Fur trader turned bootlegger ["Pig's Eye" Parrant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Parrant "Pierre Parrant"), who set up business just outside the reservation, particularly irritated the commander.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Paul,_Minnesota#cite_note-StP_PE_Schaper-17)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Paul,_Minnesota#cite_note-NPS-11) By the early 1840s, a community had developed nearby that locals called "Pig's Eye" ([French](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_language "French language"): _L'Œil du Cochon_) or "Pig's Eye Landing" after Parrant's popular tavern.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Paul,_Minnesota#cite_note-StP_PE_Schaper-17) In 1842, a raiding party of Ojibwe attacked the Kaposia encampment south of Saint Paul. A battle ensued where a creek drained into wetlands two miles south of Wakan Tipi.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Paul,_Minnesota#cite_note-18) The creek was thereafter called Battle Creek and is today parkland. In the 1840s-70s the [Métis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M%C3%A9tis "Métis") brought their oxen and [Red River Carts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_River_Carts "Red River Carts") down Kellogg Street to Lambert's landing to send [buffalo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Bison "American Bison") hides to market from the [Red River of the North](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_River_of_the_North "Red River of the North"). Saint Paul was the southern terminus of the [Red River Trails](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_River_Trails "Red River Trails").

In 1841, Catholic missionary [Lucien Galtier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucien_Galtier "Lucien Galtier") was sent to minister to the French Canadians at Mendota. He had [a chapel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Cathedral_of_Saint_Paul_(Minnesota) "First Cathedral of Saint Paul (Minnesota)") he named for [St. Paul](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_the_Apostle "Paul the Apostle") built on the bluff above the riverboat landing downriver from Fort Snelling.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Paul,_Minnesota#cite_note-19)[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Paul,_Minnesota#cite_note-20) Galtier informed the settlers that they were to adopt the chapel's name for the settlement and cease the use of "Pig's Eye".[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Paul,_Minnesota#cite_note-StP_PE_Schaper-17) In 1847, New York educator [Harriet Bishop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harriet_Bishop "Harriet Bishop") moved to the settlement and opened the city's first school.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Paul,_Minnesota#cite_note-Gilman-21) The [Minnesota Territory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minnesota_Territory "Minnesota Territory") was created in 1849 with Saint Paul as the capital. The U.S. Army made the territory's first improved road, Point Douglas Fort Ripley Military Road, in 1850. It passed through what became Saint Paul neighborhoods.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Paul,_Minnesota#cite_note-22) In 1857, the territorial legislature voted to move the capital to [Saint Peter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Peter,_Minnesota "St. Peter, Minnesota"), but [Joe Rolette](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Rolette "Joe Rolette"), a territorial legislator, stole the text of the bill and went into hiding, preventing the move.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Paul,_Minnesota#cite_note-23)

[![Image 22](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0b/Red_river_ox_cart_and_driver_in_St._Paul.jpg/250px-Red_river_ox_cart_and_driver_in_St._Paul.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Red_river_ox_cart_and_driver_in_St._Paul.jpg)

Red river ox cart and driver in St. Paul

The year 1858 saw more than 1,000 steamboats service Saint Paul,[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Paul,_Minnesota#cite_note-Gilman-21) making it a gateway for settlers to the Minnesota frontier or [Dakota Territory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dakota_Territory "Dakota Territory"). Geography was a primary reason the city became a transportation hub. The location was the last good point to land riverboats coming upriver due to the river valley's topography. For a time, Saint Paul was called "The Last City of the East".[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Paul,_Minnesota#cite_note-OAH-24) Fort Snelling was important to Saint Paul from the start. Direct access from Saint Paul did not happen until the 7th bridge was built in 1880. Before that, there was a cable ferry crossing dating to at latest the 1840s. Once streetcars appeared, a new bridge to Saint Paul was built in 1904. Until the town built its first jail the fort's brig served Saint Paul. Industrialist [James J. Hill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_J._Hill "James J. Hill") founded his railroad empire in Saint Paul. The [Great Northern Railway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Northern_Railway_(U.S.) "Great Northern Railway (U.S.)") and the [Northern Pacific Railway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Pacific_Railway "Northern Pacific Railway") were both headquartered in Saint Paul until they merged with the [Burlington Northern](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burlington_Northern "Burlington Northern"). Today they are part of the BNSF Railway.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Paul,_Minnesota#cite_note-OAH-24)

On August 20, 1904, severe [thunderstorms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thunderstorm "Thunderstorm") and [tornadoes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado "Tornado") damaged hundreds of downtown buildings, causing $1.78 million ($63.78 million today) in damages and ripping spans from the [High Bridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/High_Bridge_(St._Paul) "High Bridge (St. Paul)").[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Paul,_Minnesota#cite_note-gendisasters-25) During the 1960s, in conjunction with [urban renewal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urban_renewal "Urban renewal"), Saint Paul razed neighborhoods west of downtown for the creation of the interstate freeway system.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Paul,_Minnesota#cite_note-26) From 1959 to 1961, the [Rondo neighborhood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rondo_neighborhood "Rondo neighborhood") was demolished for the construction of [Interstate 94](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interstate_94_in_Minnesota "Interstate 94 in Minnesota"). The loss of that [African American](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/African_American "African American") enclave brought attention to [racial segregation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Racial_segregation "Racial segregation") and unequal housing in northern cities.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Paul,_Minnesota#cite_note-27) The annual [Rondo Days](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rondo_Days "Rondo Days") celebration commemorates the African American community.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Paul,_Minnesota#cite_note-28)

Downtown Saint Paul had skyscraper-building booms beginning in the 1970s. Because the city center is directly beneath the flight path into the airport across the river there is a height restriction for all construction. The tallest buildings, such as [Galtier Plaza](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galtier_Plaza "Galtier Plaza") (Jackson and Sibley Towers), The Pointe of Saint Paul condominiums, and the city's tallest building, [Wells Fargo Place](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Fargo_Place "Wells Fargo Place") (formerly Minnesota World Trade Center), were constructed in the late 1980s.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Paul,_Minnesota#cite_note-29) In the 1990s and 2000s, the tradition of bringing new immigrant groups to the city continued. As of 2004, nearly 10% of the city's population were recent [Hmong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hmong_people "Hmong people") immigrants from [Vietnam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vietnam "Vietnam"), [Laos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laos "Laos"), [Cambodia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cambodia "Cambodia"), [Thailand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thailand "Thailand"), and [Myanmar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Myanmar "Myanmar").[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Paul,_Minnesota#cite_note-30) Saint Paul is the location of the [Hmong Archives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hmong_Archives "Hmong Archives").[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Paul,_Minnesota#cite_note-ht-31)

[Operation Metro Surge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Metro_Surge "Operation Metro Surge"), a [Department of Homeland Security](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_of_Homeland_Security "Department of Homeland Security") operation involving [United States Immigration and Customs Enforcement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Immigration_and_Customs_Enforcement "United States Immigration and Customs Enforcement") (ICE) and [United States Customs and Border Protection](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Customs_and_Border_Protection "United States Customs and Border Protection") (CBP), began in December 2025, focused on detaining and deporting [undocumented immigrants](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Illegal_immigration "Illegal immigration").[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Paul,_Minnesota#cite_note-Martin-32) Initially targeting Minneapolis and Saint Paul,[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Paul,_Minnesota#cite_note-Martin-32) between 2,000 and 3,000 agents deployed in the state.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Paul,_Minnesota#cite_note-33) Activists took trainings to observe and record ICE actions.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Paul,_Minnesota#cite_note-34) In January 2026, federal officers [killed Renée Good](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Killing_of_Ren%C3%A9e_Good "Killing of Renée Good") and [Alex Pretti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Killing_of_Alex_Pretti "Killing of Alex Pretti") in Minneapolis.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Paul,_Minnesota#cite_note-:1-35)[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Paul,_Minnesota#cite_note-36) Tens of thousands engaged in mostly peaceful protests.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Paul,_Minnesota#cite_note-37) Legal challenges were filed to stop the large-scale deployment of ICE agents.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Paul,_Minnesota#cite_note-38)

## Geography

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Saint_Paul,_Minnesota&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Geography")]

[![Image 23](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6d/Meeker_Island_Lock_and_Dam.jpg/250px-Meeker_Island_Lock_and_Dam.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Meeker_Island_Lock_and_Dam.jpg)

The [Meeker Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meeker_Island "Meeker Island") lock and dam was the first lock and dam on the Mississippi River in 1902.

Saint Paul's history and growth as a landing port are tied to water. The city's defining physical characteristic, the confluence of the Mississippi and Minnesota Rivers, was carved into the region during the [last ice age](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wisconsin_glaciation "Wisconsin glaciation"), as were the steep river bluffs and dramatic palisades on which the city is built. Receding [glaciers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glacier "Glacier") and [Lake Agassiz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Agassiz "Lake Agassiz") forced torrents of water from a [glacial river](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glacial_River_Warren "Glacial River Warren") that served the river valleys.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Paul,_Minnesota#cite_note-39) The city is situated in east-central Minnesota.

The Mississippi River forms a municipal boundary on part of the city's west, southwest, and southeast sides. [Minneapolis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minneapolis "Minneapolis"), the state's largest city, lies to the west. [Falcon Heights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Falcon_Heights,_Minnesota "Falcon Heights, Minnesota"), [Lauderdale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lauderdale,_Minnesota "Lauderdale, Minnesota"), [Roseville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roseville,_Minnesota "Roseville, Minnesota"), and [Maplewood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maplewood,_Minnesota "Maplewood, Minnesota") are north, with Maplewood lying to the east. The cities of [West Saint Paul](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_St._Paul,_Minnesota "West St. Paul, Minnesota") and [South Saint Paul](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Saint_Paul "South Saint Paul") are to the south, as are [Lilydale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lilydale,_Minnesota "Lilydale, Minnesota"), [Mendota](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mendota,_Minnesota "Mendota, Minnesota"), and [Mendota Heights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mendota_Heights "Mendota Heights"), across the river from the city. The city's largest lakes are Pig's Eye Lake, which is part of the Mississippi, [Lake Phalen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Phalen "Lake Phalen"), and [Lake Como](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Como_(Minnesota) "Lake Como (Minnesota)"). According to the [United States Census Bureau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Census_Bureau "United States Census Bureau"), the city has an area of 56.18 square miles (145.51 km 2), of which 51.98 square miles (134.63 km 2) is land and 4.20 square miles (10.88 km 2) is water.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Paul,_Minnesota#cite_note-Gazetteer_files-40)

The Parks and Recreation department is responsible for 160 parks and 41 recreation centers.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Paul,_Minnesota#cite_note-41) The city ranked #2 in park access and quality, after only [Minneapolis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minneapolis "Minneapolis"), in the 2018 ParkScore ranking of the top 100 park systems across the United States according to the nonprofit [Trust for Public Land](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trust_for_Public_Land "Trust for Public Land").[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Paul,_Minnesota#cite_note-42)

### Neighborhoods

Main article: [Neighborhoods in Saint Paul, Minnesota](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neighborhoods_in_Saint_Paul,_Minnesota "Neighborhoods in Saint Paul, Minnesota")

Saint Paul's Department of Planning and Economic Development divides Saint Paul into 17 Planning Districts, created in 1979 to allow neighborhoods to participate in governance and use [Community Development Block Grants](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Community_Development_Block_Grant "Community Development Block Grant"). With a funding agreement directly from the city, the councils share a pool of funds.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Paul,_Minnesota#cite_note-43) The councils have significant land-use control, a voice in guiding development, and they organize residents.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Paul,_Minnesota#cite_note-44) The planning districts mostly represent traditional neighborhoods and combinations of smaller neighborhoods within the city.

The city's 17 Planning Districts are:

2.   [Greater East Side](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greater_East_Side,_Saint_Paul "Greater East Side, Saint Paul")

8.   [Summit-University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Summit-University,_Saint_Paul "Summit-University, Saint Paul")

### Climate

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Saint_Paul,_Minnesota&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Climate")]

See also: [Climate of the Twin Cities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Climate_of_the_Twin_Cities "Climate of the Twin Cities") and [Climate of Minnesota](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Climate_of_Minnesota "Climate of Minnesota")

[![Image 24](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/81/Saint_paul_mn.jpg/250px-Saint_paul_mn.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Saint_paul_mn.jpg)

The city skyline from the southwest in the winter

Saint Paul has a [humid continental climate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humid_continental_climate "Humid continental climate") typical of the [Upper Midwestern United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Upper_Midwest "Upper Midwest"). Winters are frigid and snowy, while summers are warm to hot and humid. On the [Köppen climate classification](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K%C3%B6ppen_climate_classification "Köppen climate classification"), Saint Paul falls in the hot summer [humid continental climate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humid_continental_climate "Humid continental climate") zone (_Dfa_ bordering on _Dwa_). The city experiences a full range of precipitation and related weather events, including snow, [sleet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rain_and_snow_mixed "Rain and snow mixed"), ice, rain, [thunderstorms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thunderstorm "Thunderstorm"), [tornadoes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado "Tornado"), and [fog](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fog "Fog").[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Paul,_Minnesota#cite_note-45)

Due to its northerly location and lack of large bodies of water to moderate the air, Saint Paul is sometimes subjected to cold Arctic [air masses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Air_mass "Air mass"), especially during late December, January, and February. The average annual temperature of 46.5°F (8.1°C) gives the Minneapolis−Saint Paul metropolitan area the coldest annual mean temperature of any major metropolitan area in the [continental U.S.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Contiguous_United_States#Continental_and_mainland_United_States "Contiguous United States")[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Paul,_Minnesota#cite_note-46)

Saint Paul is expected to be affected by climate change. More extreme heat waves are expected, as is increased precipitation in the spring and summer, which could cause river and flash flooding. Vector-borne transmission of such diseases as [West Nile virus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Nile_virus "West Nile virus"), [Lyme disease](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lyme_disease "Lyme disease"), and human [anaplasmosis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anaplasmosis "Anaplasmosis") may increase due to changes in temperature and precipitation patterns.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Paul,_Minnesota#cite_note-47)
