The **Odawa**[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Odawa#cite_note-1) (also **Ottawa** or **Odaawaa**[/oʊ ˈ d ɑː w ə/](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English")) are an [Indigenous North American](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indigenous_peoples_of_the_Americas "Indigenous peoples of the Americas") people who primarily inhabit land in the [Eastern Woodlands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indigenous_peoples_of_the_Eastern_Woodlands "Indigenous peoples of the Eastern Woodlands") region, now in jurisdictions of the northeastern [United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States "United States") and southeastern [Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canada "Canada"). Their territory long preceded the creation of the current border between the two countries in the 18th and 19th centuries.

Their peoples are federally recognized as [Native American](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Native_Americans_in_the_United_States "Native Americans in the United States") tribes in the United States and have numerous recognized [First Nations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Nations_in_Canada "First Nations in Canada")[bands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Band_government "Band government") in Canada. They are one of the [Anishinaabeg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anishinaabe "Anishinaabe"), related to but distinct from the [Ojibwe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ojibwe "Ojibwe") and [Potawatomi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potawatomi "Potawatomi") peoples.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Odawa#cite_note-2)

After migrating from the East Coast in ancient times, they settled on [Manitoulin Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manitoulin_Island "Manitoulin Island"), near the northern shores of [Lake Huron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Huron "Lake Huron"), and the [Bruce Peninsula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bruce_Peninsula "Bruce Peninsula") in the present-day province of [Ontario](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ontario "Ontario"), Canada. They considered this their original homeland. After the 17th century, they also settled along the [Ottawa River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ottawa_River "Ottawa River"), and in what became the present-day states of [Michigan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michigan "Michigan") and Wisconsin. They also occupied other areas of the Midwest south of the [Great Lakes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Lakes "Great Lakes") in what became the United States.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Odawa#cite_note-3) In the 21st century, there are a total of approximately 15,000 Odawa living in Ontario, Canada, and in Michigan and [Oklahoma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oklahoma "Oklahoma") (former [Indian Territory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Territory "Indian Territory"), United States).

The [Ottawa dialect](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ottawa_dialect "Ottawa dialect") is part of the [Algonquian language family](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algonquian_languages "Algonquian languages"). This large family is made up of numerous smaller tribal groups or "bands", which are commonly called a "Tribe" in the United States and "First Nation" in Canada. Their language is considered a divergent dialect of [Ojibwe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ojibwe_language "Ojibwe language"), characterized by frequent [syncope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Syncope_(phonetics) "Syncope (phonetics)").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Odawa#cite_note-oxford-4)

## Tribe name

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Odawa&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Tribe name")]

_Odawaa_ (syncoped as _Daawaa_) is believed to be derived from the [Anishinaabe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anishinaabe "Anishinaabe") word _adaawe_, meaning "to trade", or "to buy and sell". This term is common to the [Cree](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cree "Cree"), [Algonquin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algonquin_people "Algonquin people"), [Nipissing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nipissing_First_Nation "Nipissing First Nation"), [Innu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Innu "Innu"), Odawa, and Ojibwe. The [Potawatomi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potawatomi_language "Potawatomi language") spelling of _Odawa_ and the English derivative "[Ottawa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ottawa "Ottawa")" are also common. The Anishinaabe word for "those men who trade, or buy and sell" is _Wadaawewinini(wag)_.

[Frederic Baraga](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederic_Baraga "Frederic Baraga"), a Catholic priest and missionary in Michigan, transliterated this and recorded it in his _[A Dictionary of the Otchipwe Language](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A\_Dictionary\_of\_the\_Otchipwe\_Language?action=edit&redlink=1 "A Dictionary of the Otchipwe Language (page does not exist)")_ as _"Watawawininiwok"_, noting that it meant "men of the bulrushes", associated with the many bulrushes in the [Ottawa River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ottawa_River "Ottawa River").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Odawa#cite_note-5) But, this recorded meaning is more appropriately associated with the _Matàwackariniwak_, a historical Algonquin band who lived along the Ottawa River.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

Their neighbors applied the "Trader" name to the Odawa because in early traditional times, and also during the early European contact period, they were noted as intertribal traders and barterers.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Odawa#cite_note-6) The Odawa were described as having dealt "chiefly in [cornmeal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cornmeal "Cornmeal"), [sunflower oil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sunflower_oil "Sunflower oil"), [furs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fur "Fur") and [skins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skin "Skin"), [rugs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carpet "Carpet") and [mats](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mat "Mat"), [tobacco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tobacco "Tobacco"), and medicinal [roots](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Root "Root") and [herbs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herb "Herb")".[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Odawa#cite_note-burton-7)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Odawa#cite_note-8)

The Odawa name in its English transcription is the source of the place names of the Ottawa River, which in turn is the namesake of the city of Ottawa, [Ontario](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ontario "Ontario"). The Odawa home territory at the time of early European contact, but not their trading zone, was well to the west of the city and river named after them.

[Ottawa, Ohio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ottawa,_Ohio "Ottawa, Ohio"), is the county seat of [Putnam County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Putnam_County,_Ohio "Putnam County, Ohio"), developed at the site of the last Ottawa reservation in Ohio. There is also an [Ottawa, Kansas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ottawa,_Kansas "Ottawa, Kansas").

## Language

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Odawa&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Language")]

Main article: [Ottawa dialect](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ottawa_dialect "Ottawa dialect")

The Odawa dialect is considered one of several divergent dialects of the [Ojibwe language](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ojibwe_language "Ojibwe language") group, noted for its frequent [syncope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Syncope_(phonetics) "Syncope (phonetics)"). In the Odawa language, the general language group is known as _Nishnabemwin_, while the Odawa language is called _Daawaamwin_. Of the estimated 5,000 ethnic Odawa and additional 10,000 people with some Odawa ancestry, in the early 21st century an estimated 500 people in Ontario and [Michigan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michigan "Michigan") speak this language. The [Ottawa Tribe of Oklahoma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ottawa_Tribe_of_Oklahoma "Ottawa Tribe of Oklahoma") has three fluent speakers.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Odawa#cite_note-9)

## Early history

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Odawa&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Early history")]

### Oral histories and early recorded histories

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Odawa&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Oral histories and early recorded histories")]

[![Image 5](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2c/An_Indian_of_ye_Outawas_Tribe_%26_his_Family_going_to_War_by_George_Townshend%2C_4th_Viscount_and_1st_Marquess_Townshend.jpg/250px-An_Indian_of_ye_Outawas_Tribe_%26_his_Family_going_to_War_by_George_Townshend%2C_4th_Viscount_and_1st_Marquess_Townshend.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:An_Indian_of_ye_Outawas_Tribe_&_his_Family_going_to_War_by_George_Townshend,_4th_Viscount_and_1st_Marquess_Townshend.jpg)

Mid-18th century sketch of an Odawa family by British soldier [George Townshend](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Townshend,_1st_Marquess_Townshend "George Townshend, 1st Marquess Townshend")

According to Anishinaabeg tradition, and from recordings in [Wiigwaasabak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wiigwaasabak "Wiigwaasabak") (birch bark scrolls), the Odawa people came from the eastern areas of [North America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_America "North America"), or [Turtle Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turtle_Island_(North_America) "Turtle Island (North America)"), and from a region called [Dawnland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dawnland "Dawnland") along the East Coast (where there are numerous Algonquian-language peoples).

Directed by the _miigis_ (luminescent) beings, the [Anishinaabe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anishinaabe "Anishinaabe") peoples moved inland along the [Saint Lawrence River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Lawrence_River "Saint Lawrence River"). At the "Third Stopping Place" near what is now the [Straits of Mackinac](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Straits_of_Mackinac "Straits of Mackinac"), Michigan, the southern group of Anishinaabeg divided into three groups, the Ojibwe, Odawa, and Potawatomi.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Odawa#cite_note-hodge-10)

There is [archaeological](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archaeological "Archaeological") evidence that the [Saugeen complex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saugeen_complex "Saugeen complex") people, a [Hopewell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hopewell_tradition "Hopewell tradition")-influenced group who were located on the [Bruce Peninsula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bruce_Peninsula "Bruce Peninsula") during the Middle Woodland period, may have evolved into the Odawa people. The Hopewell tradition was a widely extended trading network operating from about 200 BCE to 500 CE. Some of these peoples constructed earthwork [mounds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mound_builder_(people) "Mound builder (people)") for burials, a practice that ended about 250 CE.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Odawa#cite_note-ONArch-11) The Saugeen mounds have not been excavated.

The Odawa, together with the Ojibwe and Potawatomi, were part of a long-term tribal alliance called the [Council of Three Fires](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Council_of_Three_Fires "Council of Three Fires").[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Odawa#cite_note-12) Together they fought the nations of the [Haudenosaunee Confederacy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haudenosaunee_Confederacy "Haudenosaunee Confederacy") (who came from the East) and the [Dakota people](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dakota_people "Dakota people").

In 1615 French explorer [Samuel de Champlain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_de_Champlain "Samuel de Champlain") met 300 men of a nation which, he said, "we call _les cheueux releuez_" (modern French spelling: _cheveux relevés_ (hair lifted, raised, rolled up)), near the mouth of the [French River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_River_(Ontario) "French River (Ontario)"). Of these, he said:

> Their arms consisted only of a bow and arrows, a buckler of boiled leather and the club. They wore no breech clouts, their bodies were tattooed in many fashions and designs, their faces painted and their noses pierced.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Odawa#cite_note-burton-7)

In 1616, Champlain left the Wendat villages and visited the _cheueux releuez_, who lived westward from the lands of the [Wendat Confederacy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wendat_people "Wendat people").[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Odawa#cite_note-hodge-10)

The _[Jesuit Relations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jesuit\_Relations "Jesuit Relations")_ of 1667 reported that three tribes lived in the same town: the Odawa, the Kiskakon Odawa, and the Sinago Odawa. All three tribes spoke the same language.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Odawa#cite_note-13)

### Fur trade

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Odawa&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Fur trade")]

Due to the extensive trade network maintained by the Odawa, many of the North American interior nations became known to Europeans by the names the Odawa used for them (exonyms), rather than by the nations' own names (endonyms). For example, these exonyms include _Winnebago_ (from _Wiinibiigoo_) for the [Ho-Chunk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ho-Chunk "Ho-Chunk"), and [Sioux](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sioux "Sioux") (from _Naadawensiw_) for the Dakota. From the early days of the colony of [New France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_France "New France"), the Odawa became so important to the French and Canadians in [fur trade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fur_trade "Fur trade") that before 1670, colonists in [Quebec](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quebec "Quebec") (then called [Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canada_(New_France) "Canada (New France)")) usually referred to any Algonquian speaker from the Great Lakes region as an Odawa. In their own language, the Odawa (like the Ojibwe) identified as Anishinaabe (_Neshnabek_) meaning "people".

The mostly highly prized fur was beaver, popular in Europe. Other furs traded included deer, marten, raccoon, fox, otter, and muskrat. In exchange the Odawa received "hatchets, knives, kettles, traps, needles, fish hooks, cloth and blankets, jewelry and decorative items, and later firearms and alcohol".[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Odawa#cite_note-14) Up to the time of [Nicolas Perrot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicolas_Perrot "Nicolas Perrot"), the Odawa had a monopoly on all fur trade that came through [Green Bay, Wisconsin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Bay,_Wisconsin "Green Bay, Wisconsin"), or [Sault Ste. Marie, Michigan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sault_Ste._Marie,_Michigan "Sault Ste. Marie, Michigan"). They allegedly did "their best to exploit" the tribes in those areas "who did not use the canoe, by bartering with them bits of iron and steel and worn-out European articles for extravagant quantities of furs". For example, "the Crees gave the Ottawas 'all their beaver robes for old knives, blunted awls, wretched nets and kettles used until they were past service.'"[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Odawa#cite_note-15)

### Wars and refugees

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Odawa&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Wars and refugees")]

[![Image 6](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/4/4b/Chief_Pontiac_%281%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail_unscaled)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Chief_Pontiac_(1).jpg)

Odawa warrior with [gunstock war club](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunstock_war_club "Gunstock war club")

The Odawa had disputes and warfare with other tribes, particularly over the lucrative fur trade. For example, the tribe once waged war against the [Mascouten](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mascouten "Mascouten"). In the mid-17th century the Odawa allied with other Algonquian tribes around the Great Lakes against the powerful [Mohawk people](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohawk_people "Mohawk people") (of present-day New York) and their Haudenosaunee allies in the [Beaver Wars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beaver_Wars "Beaver Wars"). The European introduction of guns and other weapons to some of their trading partners had disrupted the traditional balance of power in the region and changed economic risks and rewards. All indigenous peoples on both sides were disrupted or decimated; some groups, such as the Iroquoian-speaking [Erie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erie_people "Erie people"), were exterminated as tribes. But by the mid-17th century, the tribes were more severely affected by new infectious diseases than warfare. Lacking acquired [immunity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Immunity_(medical) "Immunity (medical)") to these European diseases, they suffered epidemics with high fatalities.

In 1701, the French colonists built [Fort Detroit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Detroit "Fort Detroit") and established a trading post. Many Odawa moved there from their traditional homeland of Manitoulin Island near the Bruce Peninsula,[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Odawa#cite_note-hodge-10) and [Wyandot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wyandot_people "Wyandot people") also moved near the post. Some Odawa had already settled across northern Michigan in the Lower Peninsula, and more bands established villages around and south of Detroit. Their area extended into present-day Ohio.

With movements of the tribes in relation to warfare and colonial encroachment, the tribes settled in roughly the following pattern: "Sandwiched between the French, in the north and west, and the English, in the south and east, the [Miami](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miami_people "Miami people") settled in present-day Indiana and western Ohio; the Ottawa settled in Northwest Ohio along the Maumee, the Auglaize, and the Blanchard rivers; the [Wyandot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wyandot_people "Wyandot people") settled in Central Ohio; the [Shawnee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shawnee "Shawnee") in Southwest Ohio; and the [Delaware](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delaware "Delaware") (Lenape) in Southeast and Eastern Ohio."[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Odawa#cite_note-tanner-16)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Odawa#cite_note-17)

In the mid-18th century, the Odawa allied with their [French](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/France "France") trading partners against the [British](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Kingdom "United Kingdom") in the [Seven Years' War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seven_Years'_War "Seven Years' War"), known as the [French and Indian War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_and_Indian_War "French and Indian War") in the North American colonies. They made raids against Anglo-American colonists. The Odawa chief [Pontiac](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pontiac_(Ottawa_leader) "Pontiac (Ottawa leader)")[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Odawa#cite_note-auto-18) has historically been reported to have been born at the confluence of the Maumee and Auglaize rivers, where modern [Defiance, Ohio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Defiance,_Ohio "Defiance, Ohio"), later developed. In 1763, after the British had defeated France, Pontiac led a [rebellion against the British](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pontiac's_War "Pontiac's War"), but he was unable to prevent British colonial settlement of the region.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Odawa#cite_note-19)

A decade later, Chief [Egushawa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Egushawa "Egushawa") (also spelled Agushawa), who had a village at the mouth of the [Maumee River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maumee_River "Maumee River") on [Lake Erie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Erie "Lake Erie") (where Toledo later developed), led the Odawa as an ally of the British in the [American Revolutionary War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Revolutionary_War "American Revolutionary War"). He hoped to build on their support to exclude European-American colonists from his territory in northwest Ohio and southern Michigan.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Odawa#cite_note-autogenerated203-20) The defeat of the British by the United States had a far-ranging influence on British-allied Native American tribes, as many were forced to cede their land to the United States.

Following the Revolutionary War, in the 1790s, Egushawa, together with numerous members of other regional tribes, including the Wyandot and Council of Three Fires, Shawnee, Lenape, and Mingo, fought the United States in a series of battles and campaigns in what became known as the [Northwest Indian War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northwest_Indian_War "Northwest Indian War"). The Indians hoped to repulse the European-American pioneers coming to settle west of the Appalachian Mountains, but were finally defeated.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Odawa#cite_note-autogenerated203-20)

In 1792 President George Washington sent Major Alexander Truman, his servant William Lynch, and guide/interpreter William Smalley on a peace mission to the tribes. Truman and Lynch were killed; Truman was apparently killed prior to April 20, 1792, at Lower Tawa Town, an Ottawa village (Ottawa, Putnam County Ohio). In a campaign during 1794, [Anthony Wayne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Wayne "Anthony Wayne") built a string of forts in the upper Maumee River watershed, including [Fort Defiance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Defiance_(Ohio) "Fort Defiance (Ohio)"), across the river from the site of Pontiac's birth. While the British had encouraged the Native American efforts, they did not want to get drawn into open conflict again with the United States and withdrew from offering direct support to the tribes. Wayne's army defeated several hundred members of the Indian confederacy at the [Battle of Fallen Timbers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Fallen_Timbers "Battle of Fallen Timbers"), near the future site of [Maumee, Ohio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maumee,_Ohio "Maumee, Ohio") and about 11 miles upriver of present-day [Toledo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toledo,_Ohio "Toledo, Ohio").

#### Raid on Pickawillany

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Odawa&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Raid on Pickawillany")]

In the winter of 1751–1752, [Charles Langlade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Michel_de_Langlade "Charles Michel de Langlade") began assembling an allied war party of Odawa, Potawatomi, and Ojibwe warriors who traveled to [Pickawillany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pickawillany "Pickawillany"). They attacked the village in mid-morning on June 21, 1752, and killed thirteen Miami men and captured five English traders. Down to as few as twenty warriors the Miami tried to negotiate terms of surrender, and Langlade promised to allow the Miami men to return home if they handed over the English. The Miami sent only three of the five Englishmen. When the Englishmen reached Langlade's lines, one of his men stabbed one of them to death, scalped the Englishman, and ripped his heart out and ate it in front of the Miami men. Langlade's men seized the Miami chief [Memeskia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Memeskia "Memeskia"). He was killed, boiled and eaten in front of his warriors. Afterward the Odawa released the Miami women and left for Detroit with four captured Englishmen and more than $300,000 worth (in today's dollars[_[when?](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Manual\_of\_Style/Dates\_and\_numbers#Chronological\_items "Wikipedia:Manual of Style/Dates and numbers")_]) of trade goods.

This French-led victory over the English is believed to have led to the French and Indian War and contributed to the Seven Years' War on the European continent.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Odawa#cite_note-21)

### Treaties and removals

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Odawa&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Treaties and removals")]

In 1795, under the [Treaty of Greenville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Greenville "Treaty of Greenville"), the Odawa and other members of the Western Confederacy ceded all of Ohio to the United States, except the northwest area. This was part of the area controlled by the Detroit Odawa.

In 1807, the Detroit Odawa joined three other tribes, the Ojibwe, Potawatomi and [Wyandot people](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wyandot_people "Wyandot people"), in signing the [Treaty of Detroit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Detroit "Treaty of Detroit") under pressure from the United States. The agreement, between the tribes and [William Hull](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Hull "William Hull"), representing the [Michigan Territory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michigan_Territory "Michigan Territory"), gave the United States a large portion of today's [Southeastern Michigan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeastern_Michigan "Southeastern Michigan") and a section of northwest [Ohio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ohio "Ohio") near the Maumee River.

Many Odawa bands moved away from the European Americans into northern Michigan. The tribes retained communal control of relatively small pockets of land in the territory of the Maumee River.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Odawa#cite_note-WDL-22) Bands of Odawa-occupied areas are known as Roche de Boeuf[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Odawa#cite_note-23) and Wolf Rapids on the upper Maumee River.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Odawa#cite_note-sultzman-24)

In 1817, in the first treaty involving land cessions after the War of 1812, the Ohio Odawa ceded their lands, accepting [reservations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_historical_Indian_reservations_in_the_United_States "List of historical Indian reservations in the United States") at [Blanchard's Creek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blanchard's_Fork_Reserve,_Ohio "Blanchard's Fork Reserve, Ohio") and the [Little Auglaize River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Little_Auglaize_River "Little Auglaize River") in Ohio (a total of 34 square miles or 88 square kilometres). These were only reserves, for which they were paid annuities for ten years. Pressure continued to build against the Odawa as European-American settlers moved into the area.

After passage of the [Indian Removal Act of 1830](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Removal_Act_of_1830 "Indian Removal Act of 1830"), the US government arranged for the Odawa to cede their reserves in 1831. The four following bands eventually all removed to areas of Kansas, then part of [Indian Territory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Territory "Indian Territory"): the Blanchard's Creek, Little Auglaize, Roche de Boeuf, and Wolf Rapids bands.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Odawa#cite_note-sultzman-24)

## Modern history

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Odawa&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Modern history")]

The population of the different Odawa groups has been estimated. In 1906, the Ojibwe and Odawa on [Manitoulin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manitoulin_Island "Manitoulin Island") and [Cockburn Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cockburn_Island_(Ontario) "Cockburn Island (Ontario)") were 1,497, of whom about half were Odawa. There were 197 Odawa listed as associated with the Seneca School in Oklahoma, where some Odawa had settled after the American Civil War. In 1900 in Michigan there were 5,587 scattered Ojibwe and Odawa, of whom about two-thirds are Odawa.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Odawa#cite_note-hodge-10)

In the early 21st century, the total number of enrolled members of the federally recognized [Ottawa Tribe of Oklahoma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ottawa_Tribe_of_Oklahoma "Ottawa Tribe of Oklahoma") numbers about 4,700. There are about 10,000 persons who identify as Odawa in the United States, with the majority in Michigan. Another several thousand live in Ontario, Canada.

There has been one major anthropological study of the [Grand Traverse Band of Ottawa and Chippewa Indians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Traverse_Band_of_Ottawa_and_Chippewa_Indians "Grand Traverse Band of Ottawa and Chippewa Indians"). [Jane Willetts Ettawageshik](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jane_Willets_Ettawageshik "Jane Willets Ettawageshik") devoted approximately two years of study in the Grand Traverse Band of Ottawa and Chippewa Indians community. [Ettawageshik](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jane_Willets_Ettawageshik "Jane Willets Ettawageshik") recorded [Anishinaabe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anishinaabe "Anishinaabe") stories that speak of how the Anishinaabe people related to their land, to their people, and various other means of communicating their values, outlooks and histories in and around Northern Michigan. These stories have been translated into English by Howard Webkamigada and published as the book _Ottawa Stories from the Springs_.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Odawa#cite_note-25)

By the end of the eighteenth century, the Ottawa in Ohio were concentrated in the northwest area along the Maumee River (which has its mouth at Lake Erie.)

The reservations and reserves listed below resulted from the Treaty of Greenville (1795), and following ones. These are listed by [Frederick Webb Hodge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Webb_Hodge "Frederick Webb Hodge") in his 1910 history of _American Indians North of Mexico._[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Odawa#cite_note-hodge171-26)[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Odawa#cite_note-sultzman-24)

Minneapolis[b] is a city in Hennepin County, Minnesota, United States, and its county seat.[4] With a population of 429,954 as of the 2020 census, it is the state's most populous city.[8] Located in the state's center near the eastern border, it occupies both banks of the Upper Mississippi River and adjoins Saint Paul, the state capital of Minnesota. Minneapolis, Saint Paul, and the surrounding area are collectively known as the Twin Cities, a metropolitan area with 3.69 million residents.[14] Minneapolis is built on an artesian aquifer on relatively flat terrain and is known for cold, snowy winters and hot, humid summers. Nicknamed the "City of Lakes",[15] Minneapolis is abundant in water, with thirteen lakes, wetlands, the Mississippi River, creeks, and waterfalls. The city's public park system is connected by the Grand Rounds National Scenic Byway.

Dakota people previously inhabited the site of today's Minneapolis. European settlement began north of Fort Snelling along Saint Anthony Falls—the only natural waterfall on the Mississippi River.[16] Location near the fort and the falls' power—with its potential for industrial activity—fostered the city's early growth. For a time in the 19th century, Minneapolis was the lumber and flour milling capital of the world, and as home to the Federal Reserve Bank of Minneapolis, it has preserved its financial clout into the 21st century. A Minneapolis Depression-era labor strike brought about federal worker protections. Work in Minneapolis contributed to the computing industry, and the city is the birthplace of General Mills, the Pillsbury brand, Target Corporation, and Thermo King mobile refrigeration.

The city's major arts institutions include the Minneapolis Institute of Art, the Walker Art Center, and the Guthrie Theater. Four professional sports teams play downtown. Musician Prince played at the First Avenue nightclub. Minneapolis is home to the University of Minnesota's main campus. The city's public transport is provided by Metro Transit, and the international airport, serving the Twin Cities region, is located towards the south on the city limits.

Residents adhere to more than fifty religions. Despite its well-regarded quality of life,[17] Minneapolis has stark disparities among its residents—arguably the most critical issue confronting the city in the 21st century.[18] Governed by a mayor-council system, Minneapolis has a political landscape dominated by the Minnesota Democratic–Farmer–Labor Party (DFL), with Jacob Frey serving as mayor since 2018.

Historyedit
Main article: History of Minneapolis
Dakota homelandedit
Further information: Dakota people, Ojibwe, Bdóte, and Dakota War of 1862

Two Indigenous nations inhabited the area now called Minneapolis.[19] Archaeologists have evidence that since 1000 AD,[20] they were the Dakota (one half of the Sioux nation),[21] and, after the 1700s,[22] the Ojibwe (also known as Chippewa, members of the Anishinaabe nations).[23] Dakota people have different stories to explain their creation.[24] One widely accepted story says the Dakota emerged from Bdóte,[24] the confluence of the Minnesota and Mississippi rivers. Dakota are the only inhabitants of the Minneapolis area who claimed no other land;[25] they have no traditions of having immigrated.[26] In 1680, cleric Louis Hennepin, who was probably the first European to see the Minneapolis waterfall the Dakota people call Owámniyomni, renamed it the Falls of St. Anthony of Padua for his patron saint.[27]

Dakota non-combatants interned at a concentration camp at Fort Snelling during the winter of 1862[28][29]

In the space of sixty years, the US seized all of the Dakota land and forced them out of their homeland.[30] Purchasing most of modern-day Minneapolis, Zebulon Pike made the 1805 Treaty of St. Peter with the Dakota.[c] Pike bought a 9-square-mile (23 km2) strip of land—coinciding with the sacred place of Dakota origin[24]—on the Mississippi south of Saint Anthony Falls,[35] with the agreement the US would build a military fort and trading post there and the Dakota would retain their usufructuary rights.[36] In 1819, the US Army built Fort Snelling[37] to direct Native American trade away from British-Canadian traders and to deter war between the Dakota and Ojibwe in northern Minnesota.[38] Under pressure from US officials[39] in a series of treaties, the Dakota ceded their land first to the east and then to the west of the Mississippi, the river that runs through Minneapolis.[40][d] Dakota leaders twice refused to sign the next treaty until they were paid for the previous one.[52] In the decades following these treaty signings, the federal US government rarely honored their terms.[53] At the beginning of the American Civil War, annuity payments owed in June 1862 to the Dakota by treaty were late, causing acute hunger among the Dakota.[54][e] Facing starvation[56] a faction of the Dakota declared war in August and killed settlers.[57] Serving without any prior military experience, US commander Henry Sibley commanded raw recruits,[58] volunteer mounted troops from Minneapolis and Saint Paul with no military experience.[59] The war went on for six weeks in the Minnesota River valley.[60] After a kangaroo court,[61][f] 38 Dakota men were hanged.[60][g] The army force-marched 1,700 non-hostile Dakota men, women, children, and elders 150 miles (240 km) to a concentration camp at Fort Snelling.[28][78] Minneapolitans reportedly threatened more than once to attack the camp.[79] In 1863, the US "abrogated and annulled" all treaties with the Dakota.[80] With Governor Alexander Ramsey calling for their extermination,[81] most Dakota were exiled from Minnesota.[82]

While the Dakota were being expelled, Franklin Steele laid claim to the east bank of Saint Anthony Falls,[83] and John H. Stevens built a home on the west bank.[84] In the Dakota language, the city's name is Bde Óta Othúŋwe ('Many Lakes Town').[h] Residents had divergent ideas on names for their community. Charles Hoag proposed combining the Dakota word for 'water' (mni[i]) with the Greek word for 'city' (polis), yielding Minneapolis. In 1851, after a meeting of the Minnesota Territorial Legislature, leaders of east bank St. Anthony lost their bid to move the capital from Saint Paul, but they eventually won the state university.[90] In 1856, the territorial legislature authorized Minneapolis as a town on the Mississippi's west bank.[5] Minneapolis was incorporated as a city in 1867, and in 1872, it merged with St. Anthony.[91]

Industries developedit
Saint Anthony Falls c. 1850s
Loading flour, Pillsbury, 1939. Photo by John Vachon.

Minneapolis originated around a source of energy: Saint Anthony Falls, the only natural waterfall on the Mississippi.[16] Each of the city's two founding industries—flour and lumber milling—developed in the 19th century nearly concurrently, and each came to prominence for about fifty years.[k] In 1884, the value of Minneapolis flour milling was the world's highest.[96] In 1899, Minneapolis outsold every other lumber market in the world.[97] Through its expanding mill industries, Minneapolis earned the nickname "Mill City".[98] Due to the occupational hazards of milling, six companies manufactured artificial limbs.[99]

Disasters struck in the late 19th century: the Eastman tunnel under the river leaked in 1869; twice, fire destroyed the entire row of sawmills on the east bank;[100] an explosion of flour dust at the Washburn A mill killed eighteen people[101] and demolished about half the city's milling capacity;[102] and in 1893, fire spread from Nicollet Island to Boom Island to northeast Minneapolis, destroyed twenty blocks, and killed two people.[103]

The lumber industry was built around forests in northern Minnesota, largely by lumbermen emigrating from Maine's depleting forests.[104][105] The region's waterways were used to transport logs well after railroads developed; the Mississippi River carried logs to St. Louis until the early 20th century.[106] In 1871, of the thirteen mills sawing lumber in St. Anthony, eight ran on water power, and five ran on steam power.[107] Auxiliary businesses on the river's west bank included woolen mills, iron works, a railroad machine shop, and mills for cotton, paper, sashes, and wood-planing.[108] Minneapolis supplied the materials for farmsteads and settlement of rapidly expanding cities on the prairies that lacked wood.[109] White pine milled in Minneapolis built Miles City, Montana; Bismarck, North Dakota; Sioux Falls, South Dakota; Omaha, Nebraska; and Wichita, Kansas.[110] Growing use of steam power freed lumbermen and their sawmills from dependence on the falls.[111] Lumbering's decline began around the turn of the century,[112] and sawmills in the city including the Weyerhauser mill closed by 1919.[113] After depleting Minnesota's white pine,[114] some lumbermen moved on to Douglas fir in the Pacific Northwest.[115]

Seymour Cray and colleagues began work on the CDC 6600 (pictured) in downtown Minneapolis and completed the project in Chippewa Falls, Wisconsin, in 1963.[116]

In 1877, Cadwallader C. Washburn co-founded Washburn-Crosby,[117] the flour-milling company that became General Mills.[118][l] Washburn and partner John Crosby[119] sent Austrian civil engineer William de la Barre to Hungary where he acquired innovations through industrial espionage.[120] De la Barre calculated and managed the power at the falls and encouraged steam for auxiliary power.[121] C. A. Pillsbury Company across the river hired Washburn-Crosby employees and began using the new methods.[120] Wheat farming developed west across the Great Plains, from Minnesota, to the Dakotas and Montana,[122] and new rail lines connected these farmers to the Minneapolis mills, reciprocally spurring further expansion.[123] The hard red spring wheat grown in Minnesota became valuable, and Minnesota "patent" flour was recognized at the time as the best bread flour in the world.[120] In 1900, fourteen percent of America's grain was milled in Minneapolis[120] and about one third of that was shipped overseas.[124] Overall production peaked at 18.5 million barrels in 1916.[125] Decades of soil exhaustion, stem rust, and changes in freight tariffs combined to quash the city's flour industry.[126] In the 1920s, Washburn-Crosby and Pillsbury developed new milling centers in Buffalo, New York, and Kansas City, Missouri, while maintaining their headquarters in Minneapolis.[127] The falls became a national historic district,[128] and the upper St. Anthony lock and dam was permanently closed to traffic.[129] The city announced that in accordance with a 2020 act of Congress, ownership of 5 acres (2.0 hectares) of federal land around the falls will transfer in 2026 to a Dakota-led nonprofit Owámniyomni Okhódayapi.[130]

Columnist Don Morrison says that after the milling era waned a "modern, major city" emerged.[131] Around 1900, Minneapolis attracted skilled workers[132] who leveraged expertise from the University of Minnesota.[133] In 1923, Munsingwear was the world's largest manufacturer of underwear.[134] Frederick McKinley Jones invented mobile refrigeration in Minneapolis, and with his associate founded Thermo King in 1938.[135] In 1949, Medtronic was founded in a Minneapolis garage.[136] Minneapolis-Honeywell built a south Minneapolis campus where their experience regulating control systems earned them military contracts for the Norden bombsight and the C-1 autopilot.[137] In 1957, Control Data began in downtown Minneapolis,[138] where in the CDC 1604 computer they replaced vacuum tubes with transistors.[139] A highly successful business until disbanded in 1990, Control Data opened a facility in economically depressed north Minneapolis, bringing jobs and good publicity.[138] A University of Minnesota computing group released Gopher in 1991; three years later, the World Wide Web superseded Gopher traffic.[140]

The Mississippi riverfront and Saint Anthony Falls in 1915. At left, Pillsbury, power plants and the Stone Arch Bridge. Today the Minnesota Historical Society's Mill City Museum is in the Washburn "A" Mill, across the river just to the left of the falls. At center-left are Northwestern Consolidated mills. The tall building is Minneapolis City Hall. In the right foreground are Nicollet Island and the Hennepin Avenue Bridge.
Social tensionsedit
Further information: List of incidents of civil unrest in Minneapolis–Saint Paul, 2020–2023 Minneapolis–Saint Paul racial unrest, and Operation Metro Surge
Battle between striking teamsters and police, 1934. The May (pictured) and subsequent July battles killed four men, two on each side.[141]

In many ways, the 20th century in Minneapolis was a difficult time of bigotry and malfeasance, beginning with four decades of corruption.[142] Known initially as a kindly physician, mayor Doc Ames made his brother police chief, ran the city into crime, and tried to leave town in 1902.[143] The Ku Klux Klan was a force in the city from 1921[144] until 1923.[145] The gangster Kid Cann engaged in bribery and intimidation between the 1920s and the 1940s.[146]

During the summer of 1934 and the financial downturn of the Great Depression, the Citizens' Alliance, an association of employers, refused to negotiate with teamsters. The truck drivers union executed strikes in May and July–August.[147] Charles Rumford Walker said that Minneapolis teamsters succeeded in part due to the "military precision of the strike machine".[148] The union victory ultimately led to 1935 and 1938 federal laws protecting workers' rights.[149]

From the end of World War I in 1918 until 1950, antisemitism was commonplace in Minneapolis—Carey McWilliams called the city the antisemitic capital of the US.[150] Starting in 1936, a fascist hate group known as the Silver Shirts held meetings in the city.[151] In the 1940s, mayor Hubert Humphrey worked to rescue the city's reputation[152] and helped the city establish the country's first municipal fair employment practices[153] and a human-relations council that interceded on behalf of minorities.[154] However, the lives of Black people had not been improved.[155] In 1966 and 1967—years of significant turmoil across the US—suppressed anger among the Black population was released in two disturbances on Plymouth Avenue.[156] Historian Iric Nathanson says young Blacks confronted police, arson caused property damage, and "random gunshots" caused minor injuries in what was a "relatively minor incident" in Minneapolis compared to the loss of life and property in similar incidents in Detroit and Newark.[157] A coalition reached a peaceful outcome but again failed to solve Black poverty and unemployment.[158] In the wake of unrest and voter backlash, Charles Stenvig, a law-and-order candidate, became mayor in 1969, and governed for almost a decade.[159][160]

The American Indian Movement's Heart of the Earth Survival School in 1983
General strike march downtown in 2026

Disparate events defined the second half of the 20th century. Between 1958 and 1963, Minneapolis demolished "skid row".[m] Gone were 35 acres (10 ha) with more than 200 buildings, or roughly 40 percent of downtown, including the Gateway District and its significant architecture such as the Metropolitan Building.[162] Opened in 1967, I-35W displaced Black and Mexican neighborhoods[163] in south Minneapolis.[164] In 1968, relocated Native Americans founded the American Indian Movement (AIM)[165] in Minneapolis. Begun as an alternative to public and Bureau of Indian Affairs schools, AIM's Heart of the Earth Survival School taught Native American traditions to children for nearly twenty years.[166] A same-sex Minneapolis couple appealed all the way to the US Supreme Court but their marriage license was denied.[167] They managed to get a license and marry in 1971,[167] forty years before Minnesota legalized same-sex marriage.[168] Immigration helped to curb the city's mid-20th century population decline. But because of a few radicalized persons, the city's large Somali population was targeted with discrimination after 9/11, when its hawalas or banks were closed.[169]

In 2020, 17-year-old Darnella Frazier recorded the murder of George Floyd;[170] Frazier's video contradicted the police department's initial statement.[171] Floyd, a Black man, suffocated when Derek Chauvin, a White Minneapolis police officer, knelt on his neck and back for more than nine minutes. Reporting on the local reaction, The New York Times said that "over three nights, a five-mile stretch of Minneapolis sustained extraordinary damage"[172]—destruction included a police station that demonstrators overran and set on fire.[173] Floyd's murder sparked international rebellions, mass protests,[174] and locally, years of ongoing unrest over racial injustice.[175][176] As of 2024, protest continued daily at the intersection where Floyd died, now known as George Floyd Square, with the slogan "No justice, no street".[176] Protesters continued to ask for twenty-four reforms—many now met; a sticking point was ending qualified immunity for police.[176] Minneapolis gathered ideas for the square and through community engagement construction was scheduled for 2026, with substantial completion by 2027. Applications were being evaluated for a memorial called Peoples' Way.[177]

Operation Metro Surge, a Department of Homeland Security operation involving the US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and US Customs and Border Protection began in December 2025, focused on detaining and deporting undocumented immigrants.[178] Initially targeting Minneapolis and Saint Paul,[178] 3,000 agents were deployed in the state.[179] Grassroots activists took trainings to observe and record ICE actions.[180] In January 2026, ICE officers killed Renée Good in Minneapolis;[181] later in the month, Border Patrol agents killed Alex Pretti.[182] Both were US citizens. Tens of thousands engaged in mostly peaceful protests.[183] Operation Metro Surge cost Minneapolis about $700 million for December 2025 through April 2026,[184] including police overtime, and extensive disruption to businesses by federal agents—lost business revenue December through March was estimated at $444 million.[185] Border czar Tom Homan announced the surge's end in February but in March more agents were in the state than before the surge.[179][n] While a preliminary injunction was denied, Minnesota, Minneapolis, and Saint Paul's ongoing lawsuit argues the surge violated the 10th Amendment.[186]

Geographyedit
Main article: Geography of Minneapolis
Further information: Climate of Minnesota, Climate of Minneapolis–Saint Paul, and Geology of Minnesota
The city's largest lake, Bde Maka Ska[187]

The history and economic growth of Minneapolis are linked to water, the city's defining physical characteristic. Long periods of glaciation and interglacial melt carved several riverbeds through what is now Minneapolis.[188] During the last glacial period, around 10,000 years ago, ice buried in these ancient river channels melted, resulting in basins that filled with water to become the lakes of Minneapolis.[189] Meltwater from Lake Agassiz fed the Glacial River Warren, which created a large waterfall that eroded upriver past the confluence of the Mississippi River, where it left a 75-foot (23-meter) drop in the Mississippi.[190] This site is located in what is now downtown Saint Paul. The new waterfall, later called Saint Anthony Falls, in turn, eroded up the Mississippi about eight miles (13 kilometers) to its present location, carving the Mississippi River gorge as it moved upstream. Minnehaha Falls developed during this period via similar processes.[191][190]

Minneapolis is sited above an artesian aquifer[192] and on flat terrain. Its total area is 59 square miles (152.8 square kilometers) of which six percent is covered by water.[193] The city has a 12-mile (19 km) segment of the Mississippi River, four streams, and 17 waterbodies—13 of them lakes,[194] with 24 miles (39 km) of lake shoreline.[195]

A 1959 report by the US Soil Conservation Service listed Minneapolis's elevation above mean sea level as 830 feet (250 meters).[196] The city's lowest elevation of 687 feet (209 m) above sea level is near the confluence of Minnehaha Creek with the Mississippi River.[197] Sources disagree on the exact location and elevation of the city's highest point, which is cited as being between 967 and 985 feet (295 and 300 m) above sea level.[o]

Neighborhoodsedit
Main article: Neighborhoods of Minneapolis
Cyclists on Midtown Greenway in Midtown Phillips, one of the 83 neighborhoods of Minneapolis

Minneapolis has 83 neighborhoods and 70 neighborhood organizations.[200] In some cases, two or more neighborhoods act together under one organization.[201]

Around 1990, the city set up the Neighborhood Revitalization Program (NRP), in which every one of the city's eighty-some neighborhoods participated.[202] Funded for 20 years through 2011, with $400 million tax increment financing[202] ($572 million in 2025),[32] the program caught the eye of UN-Habitat, who considered it an example of best practices. Residents had a direct connection to government in NRP, whereby they proposed ideas appropriate for their area, and NRP reviewed the plans and provided implementation funds.[202][203]

The city's Neighborhood and Community Relations department took NRP's place in 2011[204] and is funded only by city revenue. In 2019, the city released the Neighborhoods 2020 program, which reworked neighborhood funding with an equity-focused lens.[205] This reduced guaranteed funding, and several neighborhood organizations have since struggled with operations or merged with other neighborhoods due to decreased revenue.[206] Base funding for every neighborhood organization increased in the 2024 city budget.[207]

In 2018, the Minneapolis City Council approved the Minneapolis 2040 Comprehensive Plan, which resulted in a citywide end to single-family zoning.[208] Slate reported that Minneapolis was the first major city in the US to make citywide such a revision in housing possibilities.[209] At the time, 70 percent of residential land was zoned for detached, single-family homes,[210] though many of those areas had "nonconforming" buildings with more housing units.[211] City leaders sought to increase the supply of housing to create more affordable housing and to decrease the effects single-family zoning had caused on racial disparities and segregation.[212] The Brookings Institution called it "a relatively rare example of success for the YIMBY agenda".[213] From 2022 until 2024,[214][215] the Minnesota Supreme Court, the US District Court, and the Minnesota Court of Appeals arrived at competing opinions, first shutting down the plan, and then securing its survival. Ultimately in 2024, the state legislature passed a bill approving the city's 2040 plan.[216] In the years following the 2040 Plan, rent increases slowed in Minneapolis relative to comparison cities; the Federal Reserve Bank of Minneapolis pointed out the difficulty of disentangling potential effects of the plan from other market factors.[217]

Climateedit
Further information: Climate of Minneapolis–Saint Paul

Minneapolis has a hot-summer humid continental climate (Dfa in the Köppen climate classification)[218] that is typical of southern parts of the Upper Midwest. It is in USDA plant hardiness zone 5a.[219][220][221] The Minneapolis area experiences a full range of precipitation and related weather events, including snow, sleet, ice, rain, thunderstorms, and fog. The highest recorded temperature is 108 °F (42 °C) in July 1936. The lowest was −41 °F (−41 °C) in January 1888.[222]

The snowiest winter on record was 1983–1984, when 98.6 in (250 cm) of snow fell.[223] The least-snowy winter was 1930–1931, when 14.2 inches (36 cm) fell.[223] According to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, the annual average for sunshine duration is 58 percent.[224]

The Minneapolis area was originally occupied by Dakota bands, particularly the Mdewakanton, until European Americans moved westward.[230] In the 1840s,[231] new settlers arrived from Maine, New Hampshire, and Massachusetts, while French-Canadians came around the same time.[232][233] Farmers from Illinois, Indiana, Ohio, and Pennsylvania followed in a secondary migration. Settlers from New England had an outsized influence on civic life.[234]

Mexican migrant workers began coming to Minnesota as early as 1860, although few stayed year-round.[235] Latinos eventually settled in several neighborhoods in Minneapolis, including Phillips, Whittier, Longfellow and Northeast.[236] Before the turn of the 21st century, Latinos were the state's largest and fastest-growing immigrant group.[235][237]

Immigrants from Sweden, Norway, and Denmark found common ground with the Republican and Protestant belief systems of the New England migrants who preceded them.[238][239] Irish, Scots, and English immigrants arrived after the Civil War;[240] Germans[241] and Jews from Central and Eastern Europe, as well as Russia, followed.[242] Minneapolis welcomed Italians and Greeks in the 1890s and 1900s,[243][244] and Slovak and Czech immigrants settled in the Bohemian Flats area on the west bank of the Mississippi River. Ukrainians arrived after 1900,[245] and Central European migrants made their homes in the Northeast neighborhood.[246]

Chinese began immigration in the 1870s and Chinese businesses centered on the Gateway District and Glenwood Avenue.[247] Westminster Presbyterian Church gave language classes and support for Chinese Americans in Minneapolis, many of whom had fled discrimination in western states.[248] Japanese Americans, many relocated from San Francisco, worked at Camp Savage, a secret military Japanese-language school that trained interpreters and translators.[249] Following World War II, some Japanese and Japanese Americans remained in Minneapolis, and by 1970, they numbered nearly 2,000, forming part of the state's largest Asian American community.[250] In the 1950s, the US government relocated Native Americans to cities like Minneapolis, attempting to dismantle Indian reservations.[251] Around 1970, Koreans arrived,[252] and the first Filipinos came to attend the University of Minnesota.[253] Vietnamese, Hmong (some from Thailand), Lao, and Cambodians settled mainly in Saint Paul around 1975, but some built organizations in Minneapolis.[254][255] In 1992, 160 Tibetan immigrants came to Minnesota, and many settled in the city's Whittier neighborhood.[256] Burmese immigrants arrived in the early 2000s, with some moving to Greater Minnesota.[257] The population of people from India in Minneapolis increased by 1,000 between 2000 and 2010, making it the largest concentration of Indians living in the state.[258]

The population of Minneapolis grew until 1950 when the census peaked at 521,718—the only time it has exceeded a half million. The population then declined for decades; after World War II, people moved to the suburbs and generally out of the Midwest.[259]

By 1930, Minneapolis had one of the nation's highest literacy rates among Black residents.[260][261][262] However, discrimination prevented them from obtaining higher-paying jobs.[263] In 1935, Cecil Newman and the Minneapolis Spokesman led a year-long consumer boycott of four area breweries that refused to hire Blacks.[264] Employment improved during World War II, but housing discrimination persisted.[265] Between 1950 and 1970, the Black population in Minneapolis increased by 436 percent.[264] After the Rust Belt economy declined in the 1980s, Black migrants were attracted to Minneapolis for its job opportunities, good schools, and safe neighborhoods.[266] In the 1990s, immigrants from the Horn of Africa began to arrive,[267] from Eritrea, Ethiopia, and particularly Somalia.[268] Immigration from Somalia slowed significantly following a 2017 national executive order.[269] As of 2022, about 3,000 Ethiopians and 20,000 Somalis reside in Minneapolis.[270]

The Williams Institute reported that the Twin Cities had an estimated 4.2-percent LGBT adult population in 2020.[271] In 2023, the Human Rights Campaign gave Minneapolis 94 points out of 100 on the Municipal Equality Index of support for the LGBTQ+ population.[272] Twin Cities Pride is held every June.[273]

Census and estimatesedit

Minneapolis is the most populous city in Minnesota and the 46th-most populous city in the United States by population as of 2024.[274][275] According to the 2020 US Census, Minneapolis had a population of 429,954.[276] Of this population, 44,513 (10.4 percent) identified as Hispanic or Latinos.[277] Of those not Hispanic or Latino, 249,581 persons (58.0 percent) were White alone (62.7 percent White alone or in combination), 81,088 (18.9 percent) were Black or African American alone (21.3 percent Black alone or in combination), 24,929 (5.8 percent) were Asian alone, 7,433 (1.2 percent) were American Indian and Alaska Native alone, 25,387 (0.6 percent) some other race alone, and 34,463 (5.2 percent) were multiracial.[276]

The most common ancestries in Minneapolis according to the 2021 American Community Survey (ACS) were German (22.9 percent), Irish (10.8 percent), Norwegian (8.9 percent), Sub-Saharan African (6.7 percent), and Swedish (6.1 percent).[278] Among those five years and older, 81.2 percent spoke only English at home, while 7.1 percent spoke Spanish and 11.7 percent spoke other languages, including large numbers of Somali and Hmong speakers.[278] About 13.7 percent of the population was born abroad, with 53.2 percent of them being naturalized US citizens. Most immigrants arrived from Africa (40.6 percent), Latin America (25.2 percent), and Asia (24.6 percent), with 34.6 percent of all foreign-born residents having arrived in 2010 or earlier.[278]

The ACS reported that the 2021 median household income in Minneapolis was $69,397 ($82,453 in 2025), similar to the US household median income of $70,784 in 2021.[279][32] The median household income was $97,670 for families, $123,693 for married couples, and $54,083 for non-family households.[280][281] In 2023, the median Minneapolis rent was $1,529, compared to the national median of $1,723.[282] Over 92 percent of housing units in Minneapolis were occupied.[283] Housing units in the city built in 1939 or earlier comprised 43.7 percent.[283] Almost 17 percent of residents lived in poverty in 2023, compared to the US average of 11.1 percent.[284] As of 2022, 90.8 percent of residents age 25 years or older had earned a high school degree compared to 89.1 percent nationally, and 53.5 percent had a bachelor's degree or higher compared to the 34.3 percent US national average.[284] US veterans made up 2.8 percent of the population compared to the national average of 5 percent in 2023.[284]

In Minneapolis in 2020, Blacks owned homes at a rate one-third that of White families.[285] Statewide by 2022, the gap between White and Black home ownership declined from 51.5 percent to 48 percent.[286] Statewide, alongside this small improvement was a sharp increase in the Black-to-White comparative number of deaths of despair (e.g., alcohol, drugs, and suicide).[286] The Minneapolis income gap in 2018 was one of the largest in the country, with Black families earning about 44 percent of what White families earned annually.[285] Statewide in 2022 using inflation-adjusted dollars, the median income for a Black family was $34,377 less than a White family's median income, an improvement of $7,000 since 2019.[286]

Structural racismedit

Before 1910,[155] when a developer wrote the first restrictive covenant based on race and ethnicity into a Minneapolis deed,[291] the city was relatively unsegregated with a Black population of less than one percent.[292] Realtors adopted the practice, thousands of times preventing non-Whites from owning or leasing properties;[293] this practice continued for four decades until the city became more and more racially divided.[294] Though such language was prohibited by state law in 1953 and by the federal Fair Housing Act of 1968,[295] restrictive covenants against minorities remained in many Minneapolis deeds as of the 2020s. In 2021, the city gave residents a means to discharge them.[296]

Minneapolis has a history of structural racism[297] and has racial disparities in nearly every aspect of society.[298] As White settlers displaced the Indigenous population during the 19th century, they claimed the city's land,[299] and Kirsten Delegard of Mapping Prejudice explains that today's disparities evolved from control of the land.[155] Discrimination increased when flour milling moved to the East Coast and the economy declined.[300]

The foundation laid by racial covenants on residential segregation, property value, homeownership, wealth, housing security, access to green spaces, and health equity shapes the lives of people in the 21st century.[301] The city wrote in a decennial plan that racially discriminatory federal housing policies starting in the 1930s "prevented access to mortgages in areas with Jews, African-Americans and other minorities" and "left a lasting effect on the physical characteristics of the city and the financial well-being of its residents".[302]

Discussing a Federal Reserve Bank of Minneapolis report on how systemic racism compromises education in Minnesota,[303] Professor Keith Mayes says, "So the housing disparities created the educational disparities that we still live with today."[304] Professor Samuel Myers Jr. says of redlining, "Policing policies evolved that substituted explicit racial profiling with scientific management of racially disparate arrests. ... racially discriminatory policies became institutionalized and 'baked in' to the fabric of Minnesota life."[305][r] Government efforts to address these disparities included zoning changes passed in the 2040 plan,[307] and declaring racism a public health emergency in 2020.[308]

Religionedit
Further information: Religion in Minnesota
Christ Church Lutheran is one of the city's four National Historic Landmarks.[309]

Twin Cities residents are 59 percent Christian according to a Pew Research Center religious survey in 2023-24. The largest groups are Mainline Protestant (21%), Catholic (18%) and Evangelical Protestant (16%).[310] Settlers who arrived in Minneapolis from New England were for the most part Protestants, Quakers, and Universalists.[311] The oldest continuously used church, Our Lady of Lourdes Catholic Church, was built in 1856 by Universalists and soon afterward was acquired by a French Catholic congregation.[312] St. Mary's Orthodox Cathedral was founded in 1887;[313] it opened a missionary school and in 1905 created a Russian Orthodox seminary.[314] Edwin Hawley Hewitt designed St. Mark's Episcopal Cathedral and Hennepin Avenue United Methodist Church, both of which are located south of downtown.[315] The nearby Basilica of Saint Mary, the first basilica in the US and co-cathedral of the Archdiocese of Saint Paul and Minneapolis, was named by Pope Pius XI in 1926.[311] The Billy Graham Evangelistic Association was headquartered in Minneapolis from the 1950s until 2001.[316] Christ Church Lutheran in the Longfellow neighborhood was the final work in the career of Eliel Saarinen, and it has an education building designed by his son Eero.[317]

Aligning with a national trend, the metro area's next largest group after Christians is the 34-percent non-religious population.[310] At the same time, more than 50 denominations and religions are present in Minneapolis, representing most of the world's religions.[311] Temple Israel was built in 1928 by the city's first Jewish congregation, Shaarai Tov, which formed in 1878.[242] By 1959, a Temple of Islam was located in north Minneapolis.[318] In 1971, a reported 150 persons attended classes at a Hindu temple near the University of Minnesota.[318] In 1972, the Twin Cities' first Shi'a Muslim family resettled from Uganda.[319] Somalis who live in Minneapolis are primarily Sunni Muslim.[320] In 2022, Minneapolis amended its noise ordinance to allow broadcasting the Muslim call to prayer five times per day.[321] The city has about seven Buddhist centers and meditation centers.[322]
